Bio: Alan Henderson is a Chartered Mechanical Engineer and Associate Professor in the School of Engineering at the University of Tasmania. He has a strong interest and proven track record in industry-collaborative research, addressing real-world engineering challenges across the aerospace, aquaculture, and renewable energy sectors. Alan has worked as a Chief Investigator on several Australian Research Council (ARC) projects, and led interdisciplinary efforts to deliver impactful outcomes for both industry and academia.

Alan leads a research project investigating the hydraulics of dam spillways and pumped storage hydropower inlets with industry partner Hydro Tasmania. Alan is the Lead Engineering CI in the ARC Hub for Sustainable Onshore Lobster Aquaculture (SOLA). This project aims to develop a world-first commercial onshore lobster aquaculture industry. Alan is an enthusiastic educator with interests in the scholarship of university learning and teaching. He has worked as an investigator on several Office of Learning and Teaching national projects.

Research fields: Aerodynamics (excl. hypersonic aerodynamics), Energy generation, conversion and storage (excl. chemical and electrical), Fluid mechanics and thermal engineering, Aquaculture, Hydrodynamics and hydraulic engineering, Engineering, Mechanical engineering, Fisheries sciences, Agricultural, veterinary and food sciences

Supervisor: Associate Professor Andrew Trotter

Role: Associate Professor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Sub-organisation: Sustainable Marine Research Collaboration

Bio: Associate Professor Andrew Trotter is based at the Fisheries and Aquaculture Centre within the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) in Taroona. He has a diverse scientific background as a research biologist and consultant, with experience spanning aquaculture, fish and invertebrate biology, aquatic animal health, developmental biology, threatened species conservation, and biosecurity. His current research focuses on improving the understanding of life history biology, behaviour, husbandry, and culture technologies for Pacific oysters and lobsters for food production, as well as the captive breeding and culture of threatened species for conservation.
Following a BAppSc (First Class) majoring in Aquaculture at the University of Tasmania, Andrew completed a PhD in larval fish development and culture (Latris lineata) based at the Marine Research Laboratories, Taroona. He then took a gap year from research to manage the zebrafish facility at the Ludwig Institute in Melbourne. Andrew then completed four years of postdoctoral research in the Heath Laboratory at the Ludwig Institute. These studies included phenotypic characterisation and positional cloning of zebrafish mutants with defects in intestinal development. He then moved into industry where he worked as a consultant biologist at Bennelongia Environmental in Perth, undertaking environmental impact assessments. During seven years at Bennelongia he became a Principal Biologist and Director/Partner in the firm and developed an interest in conservation biology, systematics and phylogeography. In 2016 he returned to aquaculture research and is currently the Program Leader for Aquaculture Production at IMAS.

Research fields: Animal developmental and reproductive biology, Aquaculture, Animal cell and molecular biology, Zoology, Biological sciences, Fisheries sciences, Agricultural, veterinary and food sciences

Bio: Ceridwen is an Associate Professor in Architecture & Design at the University of Tasmania where she co-leads the Diverse Inclusions Lab. She has led and contributed to numerous multi-disciplinary research projects exploring how environments can be designed to be more inclusive and enabling. This has included research into independent, supported and crisis accommodation, early childhood, primary and tertiary education environments, and playspaces.Participation and inclusion are central to Ceridwen’s research. She works collaboratively with academics and practitioners across diverse disciplines, and employs creative research methods to broaden participation and foreground lived‑experience perspectives. Alongside traditional academic publications, she undertakes translational research through built projects and design guidelines.Ceridwen completed her architectural qualifications at the Edinburgh College of Art (1st Class Hons 1991) and the Mackintosh School in Glasgow (Postgraduate Diploma 1993). Bio: Associate Professor Cynthia Honan is an APHRA endorsed senior practising clinical neuropsychologist with specialist clinical training in neuropsychological assessment and cognitive rehabilitation. Cynthia's areas of research focus largely on Moderate-to-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury and Multiple Sclerosis and the cognitive and psychological changes that result from these disorders. She has a specific interest in social cognition, cognitive fatigue and cognitive biomarkers, meta-social-cognitive functioning, and functional outcomes (e.g., employment and meaningful occupation). Cynthia recently led a large national project to develop clinical practice guidelines for the management of psychosocial difficulties (relating to mental health, behaviour, and social cognition) in moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury, and is now part of a national team to implement these guidelines into clinical practice.BiographyBefore joining the University of Tasmania, Cynthia was a postdoctoral research fellow and lecturer at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) from 2012 to 2015. Her postdoc position examined social cognition disorders in traumatic brain injury and she led a large national project to develop recommendations for the use of assessment measures for psychosocial functioning in moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury. She has also previously been employed in various research and teaching positions with the University of New England, as a researcher for the Centre for Clinical Research Unit for Anxiety and Depression (CRUfAD), a joint facility of UNSW and St Vincents Hospital in Sydney, and as a statistician and research consultant for Chandler Macleod Research and Development division where she specialised in organisational psychology test development. Bio: I’m a marine social researcher, and I apply my research skills to support marine and coastal communities and sectors in sustainable transitions.I work with marine ecologists, fish stock scientists, resource economists, biogeochemists, climate modellers, political scientists and others to integrate knowledge and explore solutions.I coordinate research programs concerned with human dimensions of marine systems. 'Human dimensions' refers to communities, economies, behaviours, institutions, markets, knowledge production, other collective actions which interact with these marine systems. I design and share socio-economic and socio-ecological assessments to support public policy development and adaptive management of fisheries and aquaculture sectors domestically. More and more I work on future-facing research to support ocean leaders and communities anticipate and govern change. My research helps explore opportunities for socially responsible climate action in response to rapidly warming oceans.

Role: Associate Professor

Bio: Associate Professor Erin Roehrer is a member of the School of Information and Communication Technology at the University of Tasmania. She is a leader in designing, delivering, and advancing technology‑enhanced learning that supports diverse learners and drives innovation across transnational education contexts.

A Fellow of the Higher Education Academy, Erin brings a collaborative and reflective teaching philosophy that empowers both students and colleagues. She has led major curriculum renewals, received multiple learning and teaching awards, and serves as Associate Editor for Australia’s highest‑impact education journal, the Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. Erin is a values‑driven academic leader who embodies a “leading from within and alongside” philosophy in every role. She has held a range of leadership positions and is currently Deputy Chair of Academic Senate, Chair of the Curriculum Quality Assurance Committee (CQAC), and Associate Head Students (School of ICT). In these roles, Erin shapes inclusive student experiences, supports staff development, and champions academic excellence through collaborative, context‑aware leadership across local, national, and international partnerships.

In 2024, Erin received a Vice‑Chancellor’s Citation for Outstanding Contributions to Student Learning, recognising her transformative impact across transnational and local learning environments. She has also been awarded three Teaching Merit Certificates (2013, 2016, 2022), a team Vice‑Chancellor’s Award (2015), and numerous Unit Commendations from students. Her work is consistently commended for fostering engaging, inclusive, and high‑quality learning experiences that respond to diverse student and contextual needs.

Erin’s leadership is defined not only by her own achievements but by her commitment to enabling others to thrive. She has mentored colleagues across disciplines and academic levels, many of whom have progressed to promotion, secured awards, or led impactful learning and teaching initiatives. Her influence extends nationally through editorial and scholarly contributions, and institutionally through strategic leadership roles that shape governance, curriculum renewal, and student engagement. Her work exemplifies a values‑led, collaborative approach to academic leadership, grounded in trust, inclusivity, and a sustained commitment to learning and teaching excellence.

Bio: Dr Hossein Enshaei interest is in the field of marine technologies.Hossein commenced his career as a seafarer and has 13 years of service as a navigator on ocean going vessels. He left the sea in 1999 while he was a Master mariner to join the training institute to train seafarer and served as a lecturer and head of deck department. Upon his graduation as a naval architect in 2004, he joined shipbuilding industry and completed three unique projects. Hossein pursued his career as a maritime researcher at Newcastle University in UK while completing his PhD and served as a researcher over several national, regional and international projects while contributing to the teaching of undergraduate and postgraduate engineering programs. Since joining Australian Maritime College (AMC) in 2014, Hossein actively engaged in multidisciplinary research focusing on ship operations, developing advanced modelling, control and optimisation algorithms, and applying them to study ship’s stability and shipboard powering systems. He collaborates with individuals from different hierarchical levels and disciplines within and outside the university to enhance areas of research excellence and attract the best students and researchers from around the world. Hossein established and led a unique Real-Time Power Systems Simulator (RTPSS) facility in AMC for designing digital-twin for existing and future marine vehicles and autonomous AUVs. RTPSS not only complements existing internationally recognised AMC hydrodynamics, fluid mechanics and AUV facilities, but adds a state-of-the-art sovereign capability to Australian Maritime industry. Hossein's research interests are in ship's dynamic stability and marine informatics. He performs advanced research on ship systems, and develops decision making tools using mathematical modelling, simulation and optimisation techniques.

Research fields: Naval architecture, Ocean engineering, Maritime engineering, Engineering

text:
Supervisor: Associate Professor Ivan Bindoff

Role: Associate Professor

School: School of Pharmacy and Pharmacology

Sub-organisation: Pharmacy

Bio: Dr Ivan Bindoff is a computer scientist specialising in eHealth – the application of technical solutions to address health challenges.Working in the School of Pharmacy and Pharmacology, Dr Bindoff’s current focus is research into the use of simulations and game-play in the education of health professionals.Most recently he is responsible for the University of Tasmania being awarded the tender for the ongoing delivery and maintenance of the National Prescribing Curriculum, this is a series of interactive case-based modules which allow prescribing health professionals to explore the fundamentals of good prescribing practice aligned with the prescribing competencies framework. His technical leadership and specialist skills in this space are set to drive the advancement and modernisation of these modules, which are currently utilised as part of undergraduate training in most Schools of Medicine, Pharmacy, and Dentistry in Australia.He has also developed a novel 3D learning experience (https://www.pharmacysim.com) which helps to prepare students to go out into the workforce and face real-life situations. Traditionally, students were prepared for professional activities by doing paper-based or role-play scenarios in the classroom. Although these traditional approaches are highly valued by students, it has remained difficult to deliver enough of these exercises at the level of detail required to satisfy the needs of either student or teacher.In contrast, Dr Bindoff says, ‘Pharmacy Simulator offers a true-to-life environment where clients may be suffering, confused, angry or have communication difficulties, and where the actions of the pharmacist have immediate consequences.’Furthermore, the simulator also allows students to try again and again in their own time, either in the classroom, at home, or even using a smart phone. All without any further cost.Through a start-up company (Imitated Environments Pty Ltd), Dr Bindoff is licensing the intellectual property to institutions, with considerable interest both nationally and around the world. ‘This is a great example of progress from research and discovery to impact in the real world,’ Dr Bindoff says.The longer-term plan is to expand the application of the technology into other areas of education in the health sector and beyond. ‘The technology is content-agnostic; it enables almost anyone to write and deliver novel simulation-based teaching materials to students.’Dr Bindoff’s work builds on his career developing artificial intelligence (AI) solutions to help pharmacists in the performance of their duties. For example, he developed AI, which is now commercially available, that assists pharmacists to conduct medication reviews of patients. It helps the pharmacist manage the huge amount of data, including individual patient information, in order to identify potential drug-interactions, medications that are no longer needed and other complicated problems.He also developed Quittr, an innovative app aimed at helping people stop smoking. Other quit-smoking apps are limited: they allow smokers to log their cigarette use, gives them information about their progress, and offers tips. Quittr has the additional feature of motivational factors, such as rewards for achieving milestones that provide tangible advantages in a fully integrated game experience.‘As a model, this kind of approach can be applied to a whole range of behavioural health factors such as diet and physical activity.’Dr Bindoff is part of the Pharmacy Division’s Unit for Medications Outcome Research and Education (UMORE), a world-renowned leader in collaborative research into improving medication-related outcomes for patients. In this capacity, he contributes to the delivery of Medicines Australia’s continuing education program for members of the pharmaceutical profession, specifically in the area of understanding clinical evidence.‘As a computer scientist, it is great to have the opportunity to do work that is challenging and exciting and delivers real benefits to society,’ Dr Bindoff says.Ivan joined the UMORE group at the University of Tasmania in 2009. His early research focused on the development of artificial intelligence based clinical decision support systems to detect medication-related problems in elderly patients.He has been involved in a broad range of projects, most notably:Created an artificial intelligence based medication review system to better detect medication-related problems in the elderly.Key contributor on the $3.5M federally funded 'Pharmacy Recording of Medication Incidents and Services electronically' (PROMISe) project, in which he determined the clinical and economic value of clinical interventions performed by community pharmacists in Australia. He developed Pharmacy Simulator, a novel 3D simulated learning experience that trains pharmacy students.Lead the development of a set of student learning and student management systems to support the Medicines Australia Continuing Education Program, which has supported and enabled over 12,000 student enrolments to date.Investigator on the $3m federally funded Reducing the Use of Sedatives (RedUSe) project, which aims to improve the usage of sedatives and antipsychotic medications in aged-care facilities nationwide.Leading the development and commercialisation of Pharmacy Simulator, a novel 3D simulated learning experience for pharmacy students which is attracting interest both nationally and internationally.Leading the development of Quittr, an innovative smartphone game that rewards smokers for engaging in behaviours that work towards quitting their habit.Leading the development of a $1.13m CRC funded wound management system, that enables clinicians, clinical administrators, and industry stakeholders to better manage wounds in Australia.Leading the ongoing delivery, maintenance, and development of the National Prescribing Curriculum.

Research fields: Pharmaceutical sciences, Knowledge representation and reasoning, Image processing, Pharmacology and pharmaceutical sciences, Biomedical and clinical sciences, Artificial intelligence, Information and computing sciences, Computer vision and multimedia computation

Bio: Dr Jenna Ziebell is an Associate Professor in the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. Her research interests include the role of microglia (the brain's immune cells) in health, ageing and disease; understanding traumatic brain injury and health education. Dr Ziebell has a strong interest in how the brain's immune system is altered, or primed, with ageing or injury and how this may lead to neurological diseases such as dementia.Dr Ziebell has a long-standing interest in the role of inflammation in neurological diseases, particularly the role of microglia. She is a mid-career researcher who established the Microglia and Neurological Diseases Laboratory at the University of Tasmania. Prior to this Jenna co-established the Translational Neurotrauma Program in Phoenix, AZ, USA; where she led a research team that investigated the role of microglia in acute neurological diseases. Her interest in the role of microglia in health and disease was ignited during her PhD at Monash University and has continued throughout postdoctoral research at the University of Adelaide (2009-2011), University of Kentucky (2012), USA, and University of Arizona/Phoenix Children’s Hospital (2012-2015). Dr Ziebell’s areas of interest include microglial activation in health and disease, trauma and injury related circuitry rearrangements, microglial priming and senescence in ageing and dementia; and more recently the social impact of intimate partner violence.

text:
Supervisor: Associate Professor Mark Hinder

Role: Associate Professor

School: School of Psychological Sciences

Sub-organisation: Psychology

Bio: As people age, they experience changes in motor control (such as the coordination of their limbs as well as the dexterous control of hand and finger movements) and in their cognitive abilities (skills like decision-making, problem-solving, learning and memory).A/Prof Mark Hinder's research looks at how changes in the structure and functioning of the brain affect our ability to do these everyday motor and cognitive tasks. He examines how these changes are related to the fact that some older adults show more deterioration of these abilities while others retain a high level of motor and cognitive function late into senescence.As a motor neuroscientist, a focus of his research is to determine which areas of the brain are critically involved in the performance of everyday tasks and how these areas communicate with each other during various components of the task. He uses a technique known as transcranial magnetic stimulation (or TMS) to investigate the level of activation of different brain regions, and how different brain regions communicate, while participants perform tasks in the laboratory. By comparing the results from younger subjects, healthy older adults, and older people with mild cognitive impairment, he evaluates how the different patterns of connections in the brain relate to how well people are able to do at different tasks.‘It seems that those people who maintain better functional connectivity between different brain regions show better function into older age,’ A/Prof Hinder says.With Australia’s population ageing rapidly, his results could be important to the development of interventions aimed at maintaining motor and cognitive function, or delaying the deleterious effects of cognitive decline. One aspect of his research is to look at the role changes in brain structure and function play in dementia and other age-related conditions where people experience accelerated declines in cognition or motor function. He is also examining how the brain compensates through a process known as plasticity, for example in response to declines in function caused by dementia or stroke.‘Essentially, we are asking: when there is damage to one area of the brain, is the brain able to compensate by recruiting other areas to maintain the ability to undertake certain tasks?’Ultimately, A/Prof Hinder’s research may lead to new therapeutic procedures that use brain stimulation to help people recover motor and cognitive function. There is already some evidence to suggest an association between brain stimulation and short-term improvements in performance.‘Our goal is to understand this better and see whether we can develop therapeutic protocols that lead to sustained improvements in performance.’In his research, A/Prof Hinder has collaborated with researchers at the School of Medicine, Menzies Institute for Medical Research and the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. ‘The University has great facilities for doing ageing-related research,’ A/Prof Hinder says. ‘One of the major benefits of working here is the ease with which you can establish collaborations with world-renowned researchers in their respective fields.’ His previous projects have involved collaborations with Trinity College Dublin as well as colleagues at University of Queensland and University of Western Australia. His current ARC projects involve close collaboration with University of Amsterdam.BiographyA/Prof Hinder completed a MSc in Neuro-mechanics at Simon Fraser University (Canada) in 2003 before undertaking a PhD (Behavioural Neuroscience) at the University of Queensland (2008). He joined the University of Tasmania in 2008 as a post-doc fellow in Professor Jeffery Summers' Human Motor Control Laboratory to work on a ARC grant. Since 2012 he has been held his own research funding from ARC (ARC DP 2013, 2020) and NHMRC (Project grant, 2013). A/Prof Hinder held both ARC DECRA (2012-2015) and ARC Future Fellowships (2016-2020) before transitioning to a tenured balanced academic position in 2020.

Research fields: Cognitive neuroscience, Behavioural neuroscience, Psychology of ageing, Biological psychology, Psychology, Applied and developmental psychology

text:
Supervisor: Associate Professor Naomi Milthorpe

Role: Associate Professor

School: School of Humanities and Social Sciences

Bio: HighlightsDr Naomi Milthorpe aims to empower her students, encouraging them to see themselves as part of the university’s culture of producing knowledge. In her work in the English and Writing program, she creates innovative and challenging learning experiences that connect students with the world through literary texts. “I love working through ideas, theories and concepts in literary studies through my teaching, and seeing students do the same. I’m endlessly surprised by the ideas students have”. A collaborative, student-centred, and research-driven approach to teaching, underpinned by a dedication to scholarly inquiry and critical pedagogy, led to Dr Milthorpe and her colleagues in the English programme being awarded a Vice Chancellor’s Team Citation for Outstanding Contribution to Student Learning in 2018.Her research has focused on modernist and modernist-adjacent British literary culture, with a particular focus on satire and materiality. “I primarily work on writing that is funny, so I’m in the happy position that my research often makes me laugh out loud.”Dr Milthorpe’s career-long interest in the satirical novels of Evelyn Waugh connects her Honours and PhD dissertations, library fellowships at the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin (“I spent a glorious 6 weeks buried in archival materials by day, listening to country music by night”) and the Huntington Library, California, and her current editorship of a scholarly edition of Waugh’s 1932 satire Black Mischief. “Working on a satire prompts left-of-centre thinking on the question of what makes for a good, just, sensible, or moral life. Waugh’s Black Mischief is by no means a guide to a good life, but through exposing (and sometimes embodying) cruelty, foolishness, prejudice and hypocrisy Waugh provides an example of how humans should not behave.”CareerNaomi Milthorpe is Associate Professor in English at the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. Her research interests centre on modernist, interwar and mid-century British literary culture, including most particularly the works of Evelyn Waugh. Naomi is currently completing a scholarly edition of Waugh’s 1932 novel Black Mischief, volume 3 of Oxford University Press’s Complete Works of Evelyn Waugh. In 2018 Naomi and her colleagues in the English programme were awarded a Vice Chancellor’s Team Citation for Outstanding Contribution to Student Learning. Before joining the University of Tasmania, Naomi was a lecturer at the Australian National University, after completing her PhD in English Literature there in 2009.MembershipsAustralian Modernist Studies Network, Executive Committee
Affirmations: of the Modern, Editorial BoardEvelyn Waugh Studies, Editorial BoardAdministrative expertiseNaomi has broad experience in University administration and governance, particularly in relation to learning and teaching. She is the Course Coordinator for the Bachelor of Arts and its nested course; the Deputy Program Head for English & Philosophy; has been Head of the Discipline of English (2021-2), and has served on College and School Learning and Teaching and Academic Integrity committees as well as on University-wide Working Groups related to teaching and learning, staff performance development, curriculum management, and student management systems. From 2016-2021 she was the Tertiary representative on the Tasmanian Department of Education Curriculum Learning Area Group for English, and has served on several of the Department’s Text Selection Committees. In research, she has provided national and international research peer review and thesis examination, run professional development sessions for postgraduate students, and organised several research events.

Bio: Associate Professor Phillippa Taberlay is a NHMRC Emerging Leadership Fellow, and Principal Research Fellow and Leader of the Cancer and Genomics Theme at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research, College of Health and Medicine. Her research centres on understanding two-dimensional and three-dimensional aspects of gene control, and uses cutting-edge methods to delineate mechanisms of epigenetic reprogramming in development, healthy ageing, cancer and neurodegenerative disorders.BiographyPhillippa attained her Bachelor of Science majoring in Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology from the University of Tasmania in 2002, and graduated with a Bachelor of Science (First Class Honours) in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology in 2003. She then joined the laboratory of Dr Adele Holloway where she sought to understand how leukaemic fusion proteins disrupt epigenetic mechanisms in Acute Myeloid Leukaemia.Phillippa undertook her post-doctoral research training in the laboratory of Professor Peter Jones at the University of Southern California, USA (2008-2011). Her discovery that enhancer epigenetic states underpin cell reprogramming (Taberlay, Cell 2011) was an advance for the field that has shaped new theories of epigenetic regulation. Bio: Biotoxin management and harmful algal bloom expertise
Andreas is an internationally recognized expert in marine biotoxins, harmful algal bloom management and seafood safety. He is a Senior Research Fellow in the Health Seafood research group at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. His research focuses on understanding key physiological and cellular processes in harmful microalgae and applying this knowledge to actively improve marine biotoxin risk management and biosecurity. He provides scientific advice to SafeFish, the National Seafood Safety and Market Access program and coordinates the Australian ciguatera poisoning working group. His research directly informs risk management practices to safeguard commercially important finfish, lobster and abalone fisheries.BiographyAndreas completed his PhD at the University of Tasmania in 2017, where he explored the use of clay minerals to successfully mitigate the impact of fish-killing algal blooms. Building upon his microalgal expertise, Andreas moved to the South Australian Research and Development Institute in Adelaide, where he investigated marine biotoxins of human health significance. During his appointment as Senior Research Officer in seafood safety, Andreas conducted fundamental research into the uptake of paralytic shellfish toxins by oysters, rock lobsters and abalone to inform biotoxin risk management and validate rapid toxin test kits. He has developed a unique, high volume toxic microalgal culturing system that has been the cornerstone of applied biotoxin research in Australia, directly informing revisions of biotoxin risk management plans through improved knowledge of biotoxin uptake pathways and mechanisms. At the same time, Andreas provides scientific advice to the SafeFish seafood safety program to prioritise future research directions and coordinated the development of the Australian research strategy for ciguatera poisoning.In 2020, Andreas joined the University of Tasmania as Research Fellow in Fish Health, Biosecurity and Seafood Safety. His current work predominantly focuses on improved detection and management of paralytic shellfish toxins in Tasmanian waters. At the same time, he is building capability to quantify fish-killing algal toxins and other unknown aquatic toxicants with the use of novel cell line techniques. He continues to provide scientific advice to the SafeFish seafood safety partnership and has launched a national ciguatera awareness campaign.Memberships/Professional practiceInternational Society for the Study of Harmful Algae (ISSHA)Tasmanian Shellfish Aquaculture Research Advisory Group

Bio: Dr Bennet McComish is a Senior Research Fellow in the Menzies Institute for Medical Research at the University of Tasmania. He leads the Evolutionary Medicine group within the MS Research Flagship.Bennet's background is in molecular evolution and bioinformatics, and he currently leads a team investigating the evolutionary origins of genetic risk factors for multiple sclerosis. This work includes scanning human genome data for signatures of natural selection (including local adaptation) and modeling evolutionary processes such as admixture and genetic drift. He has worked across a range of complex diseases, including multiple sclerosis and inherited eye diseases. He manages a dedicated genomics high-performance computing cluster, supporting and training research staff and students who use the cluster. His work involves analysing genome sequence data using bioinformatic tools to identify the genetic variants that are most likely to be involved in causing disease.Bennet completed a PhD in Computational Biology in the Allan Wilson Centre for Molecular Ecology and Evolution (New Zealand). He joined the School of Mathematics and Physics at the University of Tasmania in 2013 as a postdoctoral researcher investigating the evolutionary dynamics of microsatellite sequences, before moving to his current position at the Menzies in 2016.

Bio: Dr Brooklyn Fraser is a Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Research Fellow. Her research is focused on the health and fitness of Australian children, with a strong interest in the long-term cardiovascular health benefits of greater fitness.

Brooklyn completed a Bachelor of Biotechnology and Medical Research with First Class Honours in 2015. Brooklyn received her PhD from the University of Tasmania in 2019. Brooklyn’s PhD explored the association between childhood muscular fitness and type 2 diabetes related outcomes in adulthood. Her research helped identify muscular fitness, in childhood and across the life course, as a target to help prevent type 2 diabetes. Brooklyn was awarded the Menzies Institute for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship in 2020 and a nationally competitive Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship in 2022. Brooklyn’s postdoctoral research examines the health and fitness of Australian children, with a strong focus on the long-term cardiovascular health benefits of greater fitness.

Brooklyn works with large observational studies with longitudinal data and is experienced with analytic techniques relevant to longitudinal data including life-course modelling. Brooklyn has independently developed highly engaged, impactful and ongoing international collaborations with leading paediatric exercise science experts, formalised within the Global Youth Fitness Consortium (>100 international collaborators).

Brooklyn's research vision is to establish and champion the protective power of childhood fitness to enable children to lead fit and heart-healthy lives into adulthood. She aims for her research to inform public health and clinical guidelines, early prevention strategies, and school‑based programs that strengthen child fitness.

Bio: Dr Claire Eccleston is a Senior Lecturer in Dementia Care in the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. She has a keen interest in dementia education and literacy, and in health literacy and how it can be supported by health workers. She brings experience in quantitative and mixed methods research relating to the assessment of knowledge, attitudes, and health literacy about dementia and dementia risk reduction. She has developed and validated a number of related survey instruments, and has supported their translation into many different languages. She has a breadth of experience in evaluating the effectiveness of education across multiple modes such as massive open online courses, online undergraduate courses, training of health and care professionals, and clinical placements. BiographyDr Eccleston has a PhD in quantitative ecology from Griffith University, Queensland. After returning to Tasmania, she worked part time as a Research Fellow on the Wicking Teaching Aged Care Facilities Program from 2011 to 2015, leading the evaluation component of the second part of this program between 2013-2015. The program aimed to prototype Teaching Aged Care Facilities by providing healthcare students with a quality clinical placement in residential aged care. Dr Eccleston’s work has included the development, validation and translation of a number of validated and psychometrically sound scales to investigate dementia knowledge (DKAS), dementia literacy (CAAASI-Dem), dementia risk reduction knowledge (KoDeRR), and public dementia stigma (DePSS). Claire has been a full-time lecturer with the Dementia Care degree program since 2016, and was Course coordinator of the Bachelor and Diploma of Dementia Care from July 2020- December 2023. In 2017, Claire led an investigation of dementia knowledge and education needs in the Tasmanian community and since then has been a member of teams investigating the attitudes, experiences and knowledge needs of the current and future health and care workforce. She is currently an investigator on multiple projects such as a major project to increase awareness of traumatic brain injury and the ISLAND project which aims to understand how we can promote behavioural change to reduce risk of dementia, as well as a project exploring health literacy responsiveness in the University's health and care students.Qualifications PhD, Griffith University, Australia, 2005. Bio: Damien Kingston is a Hobart-born guitarist, composer, researcher, and educator whose practice spans performance, recording, curriculum leadership, and community engagement across jazz, improvised music, and contemporary creative practice. After completing a Bachelor of Music at the University of Tasmania, Damien relocated to Europe, working as a freelance musician and completing a Masters of Music at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam (2013) under Dutch guitar luminaries Martijn van Iterson and Jesse van Ruller, following an active period in Berlin's jazz and improvised music community.

Returning to Tasmania, Damien completed a PhD at the University of Tasmania (2018) and joined the Conservatorium as a casual lecturer in 2014 before moving to ongoing employment in 2019. He currently holds three formal leadership positions - Associate Head Learning and Teaching, Course Coordinator, and Honours Coordinator - with accountability for the Bachelor of Music, Diploma of Music, Associate Degree, and Honours award courses. His teaching philosophy integrates academic rigour, industry authenticity, and inclusive practice, supporting students from diverse backgrounds to develop professional skills and discover their own artistic voice.

As a performer and recording artist, Damien has released seven albums of original compositions and contributed to more than thirty commercial releases across jazz, experimental, and contemporary popular music. His 2021 ABC-commissioned album Wells reached audiences across more than one hundred countries and was selected as Album of the Week on ABC Jazz Radio. His most recent release, Let the Light In - Damien Kingston Quartet (2023), was released by Made Now Music. Damien has performed internationally both as a bandleader and sideman, and received awards including first place in the 2016 Berlin Jazz & Blues Awards and a finalist placement in the 2013 Keep an Eye European Jazz Awards.

Bio: Emiliano's work advances remote sensing applications for mapping the biogeochemical properties of aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. He is particularly interested in retrieving fine-scale environmental attributes and understanding how they shape larger-scale ecosystem dynamics.Dr Cimoli completed his PhD at the Institute of Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) of the University of Tasmania (UTAS) working on the development of underwater hyperspectral imaging and photogrammetric techniques to map keystone Antarctic ice algal ecosystems. He has worked at the Australian Centre of Excellence in Antarctic Science (ACEAS) to design a portable acustically aided-Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) to monitor biogeochemical linkages between benthic and sympagic Antarctica coastal under-ice environments.Following his PhD, Emiliano pursued a postdoctoral research fellowship at the TerraLuma Research group as part of the Australian Research Council (ARC) Discovery project “Ultrahigh-resolution remote sensing for assessing biodiversity hotspots”. Within TerraLuma, a world-leading group in the field of remote sensing from Unoccupied Aerial Systems (UAS), he has honed his skills in a range of terrestrial applications at the forefront of sensor and algorithm development for hyperspectral image georectification and plant (functional) biodiversity monitoring.

Dr. Cimoli was awarded a prestigious JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship from the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science in November 2024 to collaborate with Hokkaido University, where he investigates Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR) imaging solutions to quantify cryogenic mineral formation within sea ice. His research integrates hyperspectral imaging and sea-ice biogeochemistry, contributing to advancements in the interactions between sea ice, phytoplankton, and carbon fluxes in polar oceans.
Before joining the University of Tasmania, Emiliano consolidated a strong civil and environmental engineering background through both his BSc (University of Padua, Italy) and MSc (Technical University of Denmark) to then specialize in the fields of optical remote sensing and geomatics. He has worked considerably in both the Arctic and Antarctic and several other remote locations providing him also an enhanced logistics and engineering background. His experiences range from technical equipment design and set-up, data acquisition, data processing and analysis up to workflow implementation and academic and public dissemination.

Bio: Gabi Mocatta is a communication and journalism researcher who currently studies communicational responses to climate change. This multifocal work takes place at the site where climate change science, public understanding and collective discourse on climate change and environmental policy intersect. Gabi also examines media representations of climate change - given most people derive their understanding of our changing climate from the media. She additionally researches climate literacy, to better understand what spurs climate action at all levels of society. Gabi is currently Senior Research Fellow in Climate Science Communication with the globally-known Climate Futures Research Group in the School of Geography, Planning and Spatial Sciences.A former journalist, Gabi began her academic career at the University of Tasmania teaching journalism. She undertook her PhD in environmental communication at the university's Media School. Gabi then worked as Lecturer in Communication and Course Director of the Masters in Communication at Deakin University, Melbourne. She has been a member of the Climate Futures research group since 2020, bringing expertise in climate communication and climate science translation for public policy making and behaviour change. Climate Futures works with with a wide range of industry and government stakeholders to deliver climate information for preparedness and adaptation.Gabi collaborates on several projects related to promoting climate literacy and action. She has worked with local government to understand and deliver climate projection needs, and to provide climate science translation for community. She also investigates the role of communication in responding to natural hazards and is a research leader for Natural Hazards Research Australia. She is also part of the team that delivers the award winning Curious Climate Schools climate literacy program for young people. Internationally, Gabi collaborates with the Media and Climate Change Observatory at the University of Colorado, Boulder, as part of the team led by Prof. Max Boykoff. This project traces media coverage of climate change around the world since 2000.

She has been president of the International Environmental Communication Association (2023-2025) and in 2025 she was elected as vice-Chair, progressing to Chair, of the International Communication Association's Environmental Communication Division.

Gabi is an Associate Deputy Editor of the journal Climatic Change.

text:
Supervisor: Doctor Gabriela Bodea

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Gabriela Bodea is a Senior Lecturer in Biomedicine and Head of the Molecular Neurogenetics Lab at the Tasmanian School of Medicine, University of Tasmania.

Dr Bodea completed her PhD with the highest distinction, summa cum laude, at the University of Bonn (2014, Germany). Dr Bodea subsequently pursued postdoctoral training at the Mater Research Institute and then at the Queensland Brain Institute, University of Queensland, Australia. During this time, Dr Bodea's work significantly contributed to understanding the role of LINE-1 retrotransposons, a class of mobile DNA elements colloquially known as “jumping genes” in generating genetic diversity within neurons during mammalian neurodevelopment (Cell, 2015; Genome Research 2017, 2022, 2023; Nature Neuroscience, 2024). In mid-2025, Dr Bodea relocated to the University of Tasmania, assuming a teaching and research role and establishing the Molecular Neurogenetics Research Lab.

Dr Bodea's Molecular Neurogenetics (MNG) Research Lab investigates the mechanisms of neural plasticity, specifically how environmental exposures shape the genetic identity of neurons and direct the formation of mammalian brain circuitry, enabling adaptive processes. The MNG team also aims to understand how environmental factors, immune signalling, and genetic predisposition contribute to complex neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative conditions, such as schizophrenia and Parkinson’s disease. To address these questions, the MNG team applies a powerful, integrated toolkit spanning cellular and molecular biology, neuroscience, and genomics. This multidisciplinary approach enables the MNG team to precisely dissect gene-regulatory mechanisms and delineate the cellular and molecular pathways that drive vulnerability and resilience in the central nervous system.

Our research has secured prestigious and highly competitive funding, including fellowships from the German Research Foundation (DFG, 2014-2016), the NHMRC-ARC Dementia Research Development (2016-2020), and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation (BBRF) Young Investigator Award (2025-2027). Reflecting the impact of our work, our findings have been published in top-tier journals, including Nature Neuroscience, Cell Reports, Genome Research, and Development.

Methods and Techniques of the Molecular Neurogenetics Lab

Mouse models (transgene, conditional gene inactivation and overexpression via CRISPRi/a, genetic inducible fate mapping)
Histology (paraffin- and cryosectioning, RNA in situ hybridisation, immunohistochemistry)
Cell culture (induced pluripotent stem cells, primary neuronal cultures, organotypic slice culture, organoid and assembloid 3D cultures)
Genomics and transcriptomics (RNAseq, DNA and RNA long-read sequencing)
Epigenetic tools (CUT&RUN, CUT&Tag)
Molecular biology (PCR, RNA and DNA analysis, gene cloning, qPCR)
Microscopy (confocal microscopy, fluorescence live imaging)

Bio: Dr. Gary Morris is a lecturer within the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. He completed his PhD in 2017 at the University of New South Wales, before undertaking postdoctoral research at University of Technology, Sydney, from 2017-2019.

His research aims to understand how the gliovascular unit functions in the healthy brain, but also how it breaks down and thereby contributes to microvascular dysfunction in multiple neurological conditions, with a focus on dementia and stroke.

Dr. Morris teaches into several undergraduate neuroscience and biochemistry units within the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre and the Tasmanian School of Medicine. He also supervises several postgraduate research students.

Bio: Greg is an evolutionary ecologist that seeks to answer fundamental questions in ecology and evolution that improve our understanding of how biodiversity is created, and how populations cope with novel environments. Supervisor: Doctor Hong Liu

Role: Doctor

School: School of Engineering

Sub-organisation: Engineering

Bio: Dr Hongyuan Liu is currently a senior lecturer in geomechanics at the School of Engineering in the College of Sciences and Engineering, University of Tasmania and an affiliated research scientist at CSIRO Mineral Resources. Hong's research interest is in the field of geohazard mitigation and prevention, computational geomechanics, tunnelling, and rock mechanics. In particular, Hong's research focuses on the development and application of advanced computational methods such as hybrid finite-discrete element method (HFDEM) in studying the fracture and fragmentation of rocks under various static and dynamic loads during tunnelling and mining, associated microseismicities, and their interactions with underground fluids such as groundwater, oil, gas and hazardous waste as well as mitigating and even preventing geohazards such as rockbursts, slope instabilities and iceberg calving. For example, Hong recently developed HFDEM and founded its website: https://sites.google.com/view/hfdem/home. Together with his team, Hong parallelised HFDEM on the basis of general-purpose graphic-processing-units (GPGPU) using compute unified device architecture (CUDA) C/C++ and developed a number of novel and efficient features, which have made HFDEM become a powerful numerical tool for investigating the fracture and fragmentation of rocks under static and dynamic loading conditions as well as mitigating and preventing the instability and collapse of rockmass structures and resultant debris fragmentation and flow process. Hong's and his team's series of research on the development and application of HFDEM has claimed a series of awards including the Top 15 Highest Ranked Paper in the 12th Australia - New Zealand Conference on Geomechanics in 2012, the Best PhD Student Paper Awards in the 3rd and 4th Australasian Conference on Computational Mechanics in 2018 and 2019, respectively, the only Excellent Paper Award in the 5th ISRM Young Scholar's Symposium on Rock Mechanics and International Symposium on Rock Engineering for Innovative Future in 2019 and the Excellent Paper Award in the 11th Asian Rock Mechanics Symposium in 2020. HFDEM is free to use for the purpose of research and/or verification although the use of the code for military and commercial purpose is prohibited. If interested, please download HFDEM and know more information from our website: https://sites.google.com/view/hfdem/home. Hong's research has resulted in more than 100 peer-reviewed journal papers including many in the leading geomechanics journals such as International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences, Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering, and Computers and Geotechnics, which have attracted a citation number of 3088 and 4111 citations and an h-index of 32 and 36 according to Scopus and Google Scholar, respectively, till June 2023.BiographyDr Hongyuan Liu's current research at UTAS encompasses the broad areas of geohazard mitigation and prevention, computational geomechanics, tunnelling and rock mechanics. He is the academic manager of Geomechanics Lab at UTAS and teaches ENG221 Engineering Geology and Soil Mechanics, ENG315/706 Foundation Engineering and Design and ENG717 Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering.Hong was a research fellow at the Golder Geomechanics Centre led by Prof David Williams within the University of Queensland before being appointed in UTAS in 2010. Prior to joining in UQ in 2008, Hong was a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Sydney funded by an ARC Discovery Project 'Effects of Tunnelling on Existing Support System' held by Profs John Small and John Carter. Hong completed his PhD at Lulea University of Technology, Sweden in 2004 and later worked there as a research scientist till moving to Australia in 2006. During the period as a research scientist, Hong, together with Profs Per-Arne Lindqvist and SQ Kou, attracted research grants of over $1M SEK from LKAB, Atlas Copco, SKB's Aspo Hard Rock Laboratory and SGU. Prior to being awarded PhD scholarships by LTU Sweden in 2001, Hong completed his Masters and Bachelor degrees at Northeastern University China in 2000 and 1997, respectively, during which, he was the early developer of the RFPA code led by Cheung Kong Professor Tang.Career summaryQualifications2004: PhD, Lulea University of Technology, Sweden 20042000: ME, Northeastern University, China1997: BE, Northeastern University, China 1997Languages (other than English)Chinese, SwedishMemberships:Committee associationsFellow of Institute of Engineers AustraliaMember of International Society of Rock MechanicsMember of Australian Geomechanics SocietyMember of Australian Institute of Mining and MetallurgyEditorial Board Members of International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Science, Underground Space and other 3 SCI-indexed journalsRegular peer reviewer for more than 10 international journals including International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences, Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering, Computers and Geotechnics, and Tunnelling and Underground Space Technology

Bio: Dr Jane Younger is a Senior Lecturer in Southern Ocean Vertebrate Ecology at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS). Her research integrates an Antarctic field program with cutting edge multi-omics approaches to monitor the complex impacts of climate change on Antarctic biodiversity, with a particular focus on understanding the threat of disease to wildlife in a changing environment. She is a 2025-26 Science and Technology Australia Superstar of STEM, a Senior Editor of Ecology and Evolution, a National Geographic Explorer, and a 2025 Young Tall Poppy Award winner.Prior to joining IMAS in 2022, Jane was a research fellow in the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath (UK). Her research focused on understanding the impacts of climate change on seabirds, through an evolutionary lens. She has also held an Endeavour Fellowship at the University of Oxford (UK) where she used genomics to examine the population structure of Southern Ocean penguin species. Prior to that she held a postdoctoral position at Loyola University Chicago (USA) and in affiliation with the Field Museum of Natural History, studying the evolution of Madagascar’s endemic avifauna. Jane completed her PhD in 2016 at IMAS, where she focused on the past impacts of climate change on Southern Ocean marine predators.

Jane’s published work spans the fields of ecology, conservation, evolution, genomics, and wildlife health. The common theme throughout her career has been understanding how environmental change effects biodiversity.

text:
Supervisor: Doctor Jayne Knight

Role: Doctor

School: School of Humanities

Sub-organisation: History and Classics

Bio: Dr Jayne Knight is Senior Lecturer in Classics and Associate Head of School, Learning and Teaching Performance in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. She researches the emotional culture of ancient Rome, with a particular focus on how emotions shaped politics and rhetoric in the late Republic and early Empire. Her monograph Anger and Politics in Ancient Rome (Bloomsbury, 2026) is the centrepiece of this program, building on her earlier work including ‘Anger as a Mechanism for Social Control in Imperial Rome’ in Emotion and Persuasion in Classical Antiquity (Franz Steiner Verlag, 2016), and connecting with forthcoming chapters on ‘Emotions in Roman Oratory’ in A Companion to Ancient Rhetoric: New Trends and Interdisciplinary Perspectives (De Gruyter, expected 2026) and ‘Senecan Strategies for Managing Envy in Early Imperial Rome’ for a planned volume on Envy in the Roman World (University of Michigan Press). Her entries on ‘emotions’ and ‘hatred’ in The Tacitus Encyclopedia (Wiley-Blackwell, 2023) further reflect her interest in the affective dimensions of Roman historical writing.

A second strand of her research examines how Roman thought on politics and emotions was received and transformed in later periods. Her ARC-funded project on Machiavelli's engagement with Roman political theory informs a forthcoming chapter on ‘Anger and Discord in Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy’ in Machiavelli and the Anatomy of Passions (Brill). Her chapter ‘The Nature and Nurture of Kingship in Virgil's Georgics and Seneca's De Clementia’ in Latin Poetry and its Reception (Routledge, 2021) analyses Seneca's engagement with earlier Virgilian ideas and imagery to activate historical memory.

Jayne believes that ancient texts speak to deep questions of human life, and one of the most rewarding things Classics can do is help students experience and appreciate the deep connections and gulfs between the ancient world and their own. She has taught ancient Roman history and culture and Latin language units at all levels. Her commitment to expanding access for students has driven sustained innovation in blended and online learning, recognised by multiple University of Tasmania Teaching Merit Certificates, a Student Focus Award, and a Team Citation for Outstanding Contributions to Student Learning. She has also contributed extensively to curriculum development at unit, major, and course level, including serving as Course Coordinator for the Bachelor of Arts with Honours and Assistant Dean, Distinctiveness and Innovation in the former College of Arts, Law and Education.

Bio: Jessica Urwin is Lecturer in Environmental History in the School of Humanities, College of Arts, Law and Education. Her research interests and expertise span nuclear history, Australian history, environmental history, colonial and imperial history, and environmental justice. Her award-winning doctoral research, completed at the Australian National University, explored the relationship between nuclear processes (including radium and uranium mining, nuclear weapons testing, and nuclear waste dumping) and colonialism in Australia. Her first monograph, Contaminated Country: Nuclear Colonialism and Aboriginal Resistance in Australia, was published in the University of Washington Press' Weyehaeuser Environmental Books series in September 2025 and an Australian edition is set to be published by Melbourne University Press in 2026.

Jess is a member of the Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand Environmental History Network's steering committee, an editorial board member of Global Environment, and a Friend of the Centre for Environmental History at ANU.

Research Interests

Jess' research interests span across Australian scientific, environmental, political, and colonial history. Her immediate field of expertise is in Australian nuclear, colonial, and environmental histories, but she has also worked on historical research concerned with the Murray-Darling Basin and other 'watery spaces', oral history, global environmental history, and the history of science and scientific networks in Australia and beyond.

Expanding upon her work into nuclear colonialism, Jess is interested in Australian mining history, and hopes to engage critically with the industry's environmental and colonial dimensions, from settlement through to the present. In particular, she is interested in the politics of mineral extraction, from understanding the 'roots' of settlers' engagements with mining (in particular of radioactive minerals), to tracing the 'routes' of mined minerals across the world, to grappling with mining's more recent interactions with Indigenous land rights and conservation debates.

Teaching Summary

Jess is passionate about providing inclusive and accessible education to her students. She has taught global imperial history, Australian colonial history, and global environmental history, and provided mentorship to undergraduate, Honours and PhD students. She is the current coordinator of HASS Honours, and unit coordinator of HUM410: Contemporary Humanities Research, HUM405: Advanced Reading Seminar, HUM419: Advanced Text-Based Reading Seminar, HAA106: Oral History, and HTA348: Global Environmental History (alongside A/Prof Alessandro Antonello).

Research fields: Environmental history, Australian history, History of empires, imperialism and colonialism, Historical studies, History, heritage and archaeology

Supervisor: Doctor Juan Afonso

Role: Doctor

School: University of Tasmania

Sub-organisation: Earth Sciences/CODES

Bio: A/Prof. Juan C. Afonso's background is in computational geoscience and geodata integration. After graduating with a PhD in theoretical geophysics at Carleton University, Juan C. Afonso undertook postdoctoral research at the Institute of Earth Sciences Jaume Almera (CSIC, Barcelona) on the development of new methods to study the thermal and compositional structures of the lithospheric/sublithospheric upper mantle. He subsequently joined Macquarie University in 2009 as part of the recruitment program CoRE (Concentration of Research Excellence). In 2022, he joined the ITC Faculty (University of Twente, Netherlands) as full-time staff. In 2026 he joined the School of Natural Sciences at the University of Tasmania. He was an Adjunct Professor at the Centre for Earth Evolution and Dynamics (CEED, University of Oslo) and Honorary Professor at the Dept. of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Macquarie University. He currently is a Visiting Professor in the Department of Earth and Space Sciences at SUSTech University and in ITC at the University of Twente.

Dr Afonso's current research includes the development of methodologies (and associated computational tools) that formally combine geophysics, numerical modelling, petrology and geochemistry to obtain reliable and realistic models of the Earth's interior using satellite-derived and land-based data sets. For this (and related) work he has received the 2013 EGU Outstanding Young Scientist Award (Geodynamics Division), the 2017 Anton Hales Medal of the Australian Academy of Sciences and the 2019 IUGG Early Career Scientist Award, among others.

His research centers on understanding the thermochemical structure and evolution of the lithosphere, as well as the mechanical and geochemical interactions between tectonic plates and the sublithospheric upper mantle. His work explores how these interactions influence both regional and global tectonic processes, with implications for plate dynamics, mantle convection, and crustal evolution.
​​
His most recent research integrates machine learning, multiscale probabilistic inversion, and numerical modeling to investigate some of the most fundamental questions about the nature and evolution of the lithosphere and upper mantle using a formal combination of multiple satellite (e.g. gravity, magnetic field) and land-based (e.g. geochemistry, seismic) data sets.
​​
He also works on the development of novel numerical algorithms to model the complex coupling between geodynamic and geochemical processes. This work directly supports the global energy transition by enabling more accurate and physically realistic models for geothermal resource assessment and critical mineral exploration. His methodologies assist in identifying subsurface conditions favorable for sustainable energy development and securing the raw materials essential for clean energy technologies.

Currently, Dr. Afonso is the leader and coordinator of the following large projects:
​
- The EU Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network EarthSafe: Unveiling Earth's Critical Resources for Clean Energy and a Sustainable Future (https://earthsafe-dn.eu/)
​
- The passive seismic experiment PatagoniARRAY (imaging and modelling the Patagonian lithosphere)
​
- The NWO DeepNL Project INTEGRATION (Integrated subsurface modelling beneath Groningen and on-shore Netherlands from multi-data probabilistic inversions; link)
​
He also enjoys very much spending quality time with his family and playing drums whenever possible...

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Karelle Siellez is an astrophysicist and Lecturer in Physics at the University of Tasmania. Her research focuses on transient and multi-messenger astrophysics, including gamma-ray bursts, kilonovae, supernovae, gravitational-wave counterparts, and rapid optical follow-up of short-lived cosmic explosions. Her work connects high-energy space missions, gravitational-wave observatories, and ground-based telescope networks to understand some of the most energetic events in the Universe.
Before joining UTAS, Dr Siellez contributed to major international collaborations including LIGO/Virgo and Fermi/GBM. She developed and led work on subthreshold gamma-ray burst searches associated with gravitational-wave events, contributing to the scientific context of the first joint gravitational-wave and electromagnetic detection, GW170817/GRB 170817A. This discovery transformed the field by confirming that neutron-star mergers can produce both gravitational waves and light, and that they are sites of heavy-element production in the Universe. As part of the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, she shared in the 2017 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics.
At UTAS, Dr Siellez is developing a research, teaching and engagement program centred on southern-hemisphere transient astronomy. Her work aims to strengthen the role of Tasmanian optical facilities in rapid follow-up of gamma-ray bursts, kilonovae and gravitational-wave counterparts, while creating student pathways into real astronomical research. She is involved in national and international initiatives linked to SVOM, Rubin Observatory/LSST, OzGrav, robotic telescope networks and time-domain astronomy.
Dr Siellez is also a committed science communicator who connects physics with storytelling, music, visual art and public engagement. She has delivered public talks and outreach activities across Australia, France, French Polynesia and the United States, including schools, festivals, public lectures and interdisciplinary science-art events. Her engagement work includes gravitational-wave sonification, astronomy-inspired painting, dark-sky advocacy, and public programs highlighting the scientific, cultural and environmental importance of Tasmania’s skies.

Research fields: General relativity and gravitational waves, High energy astrophysics and galactic cosmic rays, Cosmology and extragalactic astronomy, Astronomical instrumentation, Astronomical sciences, Physical sciences

text:
Supervisor: Doctor Ke Liu

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Ke Liu has established an internationally recognised research profile in climate adaptation science and agricultural systems modelling. His work has significantly advanced the representation of soil waterlogging stress in many farming systems models, repositioning waterlogging from a historically under-represented agronomic constraint to a quantifiable and scenario-testable climate risk within mainstream process-based crop modelling frameworks. He led the development and implementation of generic waterlogging algorithms within internationally recognised modelling platforms (APSIM Classic/Next Generation, DSSAT and SWAGMAN Destiny), enabling cross-regional and scenario-based risk quantification. These tools have been adopted within collaborative modelling programs and decision-support frameworks used in more than 30 countries, supporting improved assessment of soil waterlogging stress in climate impact analyses.
His 2023 Nature Communications paper, “Silver lining to a climate crisis in multiple prospects for alleviating crop waterlogging under future climates,” provided the first global-scale quantification of current and future waterlogging risk and mitigation potential and has helped catalyse broader research attention to waterlogging risk in climate impact assessments. This paper was featured by the journal under its Earth and Environmental Sciences Highlights and has been cited over 250 times and recognised as a Highly Cited Paper in the Web of Science. In recognition of the study’s significant impact, Dr. Liu was invited by the Nature editorial team to create a popular science video in 2024. The video has garnered more than 15,000 views on YouTube, reflecting the broad interest and influence of his research within the scientific community.
Dr Liu has also been invited to co-lead the AgMIP waterlogging initiative, a leading international platform dedicated to harmonising soil waterlogging stress representation across crop models. This collaboration culminated in a Nature Food review, “Gaps and strategies for accurate simulation of waterlogging impacts on crop productivity”, published in 2025, which identified key knowledge gaps and strategic pathways for advancing waterlogging simulation and modelling standards internationally, further advancing the global understanding and modeling of waterlogging effects on agricultural systems.
Since 2019, Dr Liu has published more than 110 refereed papers (35+ as first or corresponding author), ranked the 5th among the top 500 authors at the University of Tasmania (2022–2025) by scholarly output, with 4, 200+ citations and H-index of 37, Stanford/Elsevier's Top 2% Scientist Rankings (2025). Most of the papers published in prestigious journals such as Nature Food (2026, 2025, 2024) and Nature Communications (2026, 2023). These high-impact contributions reflect Dr. Liu’s strong commitment to research excellence, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and real-world impact, solidifying his reputation as a thought leader in the field of sustainable agriculture.

Bio: Dr Kyra Wood is an experienced academic and research project manager with a professional background in architecture and design. Her current research focusses on timber design and products at the University of Tasmania’s Centre for Sustainable Architecture with Wood. She works regularly with partners in the Australian timber and construction industries as well as several interstate and overseas research institutions.Kyra supervises post-graduate students at the University of Tasmania and as an adjunct at the University of the Sunshine Coast and is passionate about supporting early career researchers and postgraduate students to thrive in their chosen fields of research.BiographyPrior to commencing work as a timber researcher, Kyra worked as a registered architect in Adelaide (not currently practicing). Although her research focus is currently on timber design and products, she maintains an ongoing interest in critical design ethnography and applies her background experience in collaborative design engagement in cross-cultural contexts to her current role managing various research projects that straddle the needs of the timber and design communities, where similarly complex challenges and diverse stakeholder groups exist.Kyra joined the Centre for Sustainable Architecture with Wood in 2018, and was quickly recruited as the principal researcher and team leader for two Launceston-based National Institute for Forest Products Innovation (NIFPI) projects focusing on timber durability. These pilot NIFPI projects were jointly funded by the Federal Government, state governments and industry to support small-scale, short-term collaborative research, and in 2022, the Australian Federal Government committed a further $100 million to a major Australian Forest and Wood Innovations (AFWI) program in Australia for ongoing research over the next 4-5 years that directly builds on the successes of three pilot NIFPI centres – in Launceston, Mount Gambier and Gippsland.In 2022, Kyra was nominated and selected as the inaugural Australian Ambassador for Women in Wood Science by the International Society of Wood Science and Technology (SWST) and joined the regional research collaboration program (RRC) as a Research Fellow, before a period of parental leave in 2023. She returned in 2024 to work on the development of a new AFWI centre application on supporting the timber industry's appearance products sector during the transition to an increased reliance on plantation and other younger hardwood resources. Her research focuses on a range of environmental exposures, including ambient air pollution, wildfire smoke, greenness, and pesticide exposure. Dr Scheepers is the Lead of the Early‑Life Follow‑up (ELF) Stream of the Hazelwood Health Study, where she investigates the long-term cardiorespiratory, health and development of children exposed to a severe pollution event associated with a coal mine fire during their first 1000 days of life. She also provides scientific and operational leadership for the Statins Against Bushfire Smoke (SABS) clinical trial, which is testing whether interventions can reduce the cardiovascular impacts of wildfire smoke exposure.
She is always interested in hearing from motivated Honours and PhD students who would like to work on environmental exposures and early‑life health using large population datasets.

Bio: Dr McCallum is an expert in the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique. 'In VLBI we use signals from far distant radio galaxies to measure the Earth. In more detail, VLBI is used to measure the Earth's shape, the rotation of the Earth, polar motion, plate tectonics and the variation of these effects.'Dr. McCallum is the project scientist in the AuScope VLBI project, a research collaboration with Geoscience Australia, as part of the Positioning Australia project. She uses the university's own radio telescopes at Mt. Pleasant, the Northern Territory and in Western Australia, in common measurements together with telescopes all over the world. The goals of the VLBI group at UTAS are to guarantee best possible performance of our telescopes in global observations and to develop new methods to implement the next generation VLBI global observing system (VGOS). VGOS will be able to measure global distances to the level of a few millimetres, a necessity for important scientific and societal questions in geosciences, as for example the prediction of sea level rise of a few mm per year.VLBI is a key technique for measuring the Terrestrial Reference Frame (TRF), the Earth’s most precise coordinate system. Dr McCallum’s research focuses in the field of space ties, meaning that she tries to connect the geodetic techniques of the Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS, GPS), Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) and VLBI directly via a single satellite platform. Essential for space ties is VLBI satellite tracking. VLBI observations to satellites is an exciting and new technique, and Dr McCallum is leading an ARC DECRA project in this area.CareerDr Lucia McCallum is a Geodesist at the School of Physical Science, working in the group of radio astronomy. Bio: I'm the Associate Head of School for Learning and Teaching in the School of Geography, Planning and Spatial Sciences. I lead a team of exceptional people who are experts in nature conservation, climate science, landscape restoration, measuring and monitoring the natural environment, and making planful decisions that enhance sustainability and life on land. Our team teach in exciting ways and want to bring opportunities to learners worldwide via Tasmania's landscapes as living laboratories, irrespective of whether this is online or here in Hobart.

I'm an abiotic physical geographer who works in commodities (agriculture, forestry, mineral resources, geotourism) and nature (geo)conservation. My work is applied to geoheritage conservation and environmental education and extension. My contributions have been instrumental in advancing understanding of geoconservation theory and practise, and the management of geodiversity. I deliver Australia's sole undergraduate and postgraduate units in geoheritage and geotourism, bridging the gap between outdoor recreation, production landscapes and protected areas conservation practice. I'm passionate about bringing the cummulative expertise of my industry and practitioner networks into the classroom, where I use virtual and Tasmanian landscape exploration and professional training to build confidence, workforce capability and geographic knowledge.

My research is all about geoconservation. I have built a team of geoconservation researchers and practitioners who use and develop Tools for Abiotic Research in Nature (TARN). We examine and protect the values of cultural landscapes, develop digital tools to support geoconservation protections in UNESCO Global Geoparks, and examine degradation risks from natural hazards to geodiversity and geoheritage in protected areas. The tools that we create are sometimes instruments or new technologies, and sometimes they are decision-support frameworks or new processes for people managing soils, waterways, landforms and heritage places. I have managerial and/or leadership expertise in industry, government and academia. My strengths are in the coordination of large, inter-disciplinary teams, change management, advocacy, strategy, and managing for diversity. I think it takes many different types of people to solve problems, and I encourage my teams to contribute their diverse talents alongside industry and community. There are collaborative approaches to solve problems that balance the needs of humans and nature, and I like to bring people together to make this happen.

text:

Role: Doctor

Bio: I am a marine scientist specialising in fisheries assessment, population ecology, and spatial data analysis. My current work at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS), University of Tasmania, focuses on assessing the status of key Tasmanian fisheries—including scalefish, Southern Calamari, and Pale Octopus—using analytical, model-based, and empirical approaches to evaluate stock trends, fishing pressure, and sustainability. I routinely provide science-based advice to government and industry through technical reports, working groups, and briefings.

My expertise spans stock assessment methods including CPUE standardization, surplus production models (CMSY, BSM, OCOM), and statistical modelling using GAMs and GLMs. I am highly proficient in R programming for data analysis and visualization, and experienced with GIS platforms (ArcGIS, QGIS) for spatial analysis of marine populations and fisheries.

My earlier career centered on marine vertebrate ecology, particularly the movements, habitat use, and population dynamics of seals and seabirds in relation to offshore energy infrastructure. This research, developed through positions at world-class institutions including the Sea Mammal Research Unit (University of St Andrews), CSIRO Oceans and Atmosphere, and IMAS, provides a strong foundation for understanding fish population dynamics within broader ecosystem contexts. Across academic, government, and consultancy roles, I have developed broad expertise in species distribution modelling, satellite telemetry, and the integration of ecological and human-use datasets.

I am committed to producing clear, defensible science that supports evidence-based management of marine resources and contributes to improved understanding of marine ecosystems.
