text:
Supervisor: Doctor Ryan Day

Role: Doctor

Bio: Ryan Day is Senior Research Fellow in Marine Animal Physiology and Biochemistry at University of Tasmania’s Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. In 2003, he received a Bachelor of Arts - Biology from the University of Chicago. In 2006, he received a Bachelor of Science - Marine Biology from the University of Queensland and in 2012, he received his PhD in Zoology from the University of Queensland.

Ryan has been a researcher at IMAS since 2012. One of his primary research areas are in measuring the impact of seismic surveys on marine invertebrates. In this field, his research has used quantification of acid-base physiology, haemolymph electrolyte and mineral homeostasis, immune function and oxidative stress to assess the health status of marine invertebrates including lobster, scallops and octopus to evaluate the impact of exposure to seismic air gun signals. The outcomes of this research have been incorporated by the federal regulatory body (NOPSEMA) for impact assessments to minimise harm to marine life.

In his second primary research area, Ryan investigates approaches for improving invertebrate fishery practices and outcomes, with a current focus on the commercial scallop. This research developed in response to reports of large-scale mortalities within the scallop fishery. In conducting an assessment of haemolymph physiology, including biochemistry and immune function, his research aims to identify environmental stressors underlying mortality to provide fishery management with options for responding to bed die offs. In similar work with the Southern Rock Lobster fishery response, Ryan authored an industry best practices guide with recommendations on handling and water quality management. Implementation of these recommendations has been attributed to eliminating mass mortality events and halving mortality rates by industry partners. This work has recently been extended to the fishing vessel component of the industry and projects to apply this research to other marine invertebrate fisheries are in development. In addition to his recent work with invertebrates, Ryan’s PhD research focused on digestive physiology in marine fishes, in which he characterised digestive strategies in fishes that lack a stomach.

Research fields: Animal structure and function, Aquaculture and fisheries stock assessment, Invertebrate biology, Zoology, Biological sciences, Fisheries sciences, Agricultural, veterinary and food sciences

Bio: Dr Santosh Kisan Pagire is a Research Fellow at the University of Tasmania (Australia), working with Prof. Alex C. Bissember on multiple ARC-funded programs in light-driven catalysis. He also serves as Assistant Professor of Chemistry at Indian Institute of Technology, Banaras Hindu University (IIT–BHU), Varanasi (India).

Born in Maharashtra (India), Santosh’s academic trajectory transformed early in his BSc when disciplined mentorship from Prof. Dilip R. Thube and Prof. Tukaram S. Thopate ignited his passion for synthetic organic chemistry, particularly for organic reaction mechanisms. Rising from a below-average student to one of the top three in his class at the New Arts, Commerce, and Science College, Parner, he also ranked 5th in Chemistry across all colleges under the University of Pune in 2009.

During his Master’s degree at the Department of Chemistry, University of Pune (2009–2011), he received the Eklavya (merit) and Kawathekar (need-cum-merit) fellowships. In 2010, he qualified the MH-SET (Maharashtra State Eligibility Test) on his first attempt, and in 2011, he secured a highly competitive All-India Rank of 22 (top 1%) in the CSIR–NET examination—again on the first attempt. He trained under distinguished teachers, including Prof. Murzban S. Wadia, Prof. Mukund G. Kulkarni, and Prof. Shridhar R. Gadre, with exceptional mentorship from Prof. Dilip D. Dhavale FASc (Head and Distinguished Professor, Department of Chemistry, University of Pune).

Immediately after his Master’s in 2011, Santosh dedicated a few months to teaching chemistry free of charge to rural students at Dhokeshwar Mahavidyalaya in Maharashtra (Affil. University of Pune)—an experience that strengthened his communication, empathy, and commitment to accessible science education.

In 2011–2013, he undertook early research training in asymmetric organocatalysis, international metal catalysis work with Prof. Pher G. Andersson (Sweden) and Prof. Thavendran Govender (South Africa), and advanced total-synthesis training at NCL Pune (India) with Dr Subhash P. Chavan. This broad foundation led to multiple international PhD offers, independent of fellowship outcomes.

In 2013, he secured the prestigious DAAD Fellowship—on his first attempt—to pursue a PhD in Synthetic Organic Chemistry at the University of Regensburg (Germany) under Prof. Oliver Reiser, completing his doctorate in December 2017.
Following his PhD, Santosh obtained the postdoctoral positions he most aspired to, and once again the associated elite international fellowships were awarded to his research proposals on the first attempt. His postdoctoral research included:• DFG Walter Benjamin Postdoctoral Fellow, BIKAKEN (Affil. The University of Tokyo, Japan) with Profs. Masakatsu Shibasaki and Naoya Kumagai (2018–2021);• Marie Skłodowska–Curie Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Bristol—ranked #1 in the UK for Chemistry (REF 2021)—with Prof. Varinder K. Aggarwal FRS (2021–2023);• followed by a research stay with Prof. Lutz Ackermann, University of Göttingen, Germany (2023–2024).

In 2024–2025, he transitioned to industry, leading a Discovery Chemistry group at Syngene International Ltd., India, for Kestrel Therapeutics (USA), contributing to early-stage drug discovery. In March 2025, he joined Chanakya University, where his clear, application-focused teaching approach transformed initially uninterested BTech engineering students into highly engaged learners—earning him the highest teaching feedback ratings across the cohort. He moved to the University of Tasmania (Australia) in September 2025 to resume his research journey.

Santosh’s research integrates visible- and near-infrared (NIR) photocatalysis, radical chemistry, asymmetric synthesis, and phosphorus chemistry to develop selective and sustainable molecular transformations. He has published in leading journals, including Accounts of Chemical Research (IF ~24.6), Angewandte Chemie International Edition (16.8), Journal of the American Chemical Society (16.4), and ACS Catalysis (13.7), and has accumulated >3,300 citations, with a strong first-author record in top-tier Q1 journals.

text:
Supervisor: Doctor Sara Karacsony

Role: Doctor

School: School of Nursing

Bio: I am a nursing academic researcher in the fields of palliative care and aged care and an active member of the Transforming Research in Ageing (TRiA) group within the school of Nursing at the University of Tasmania. My research and teaching areas focus on workforce education and skills development in palliative care, and care and quality of life of older people. I joined the project team on the first Australian-funded research study into the benefits of the multisensory, psychosocial Namaste Care program for people living with advanced dementia in residential aged care facilities and continue to promote the program’s philosophy and principles into various contexts of care as the Australian champion for Namaste Care International. My focus is on developing skilled, compassionate palliative care nurses (and care staff) within aged care and nursing graduands who are invested in evidence-informed practice. I endeavour to set students up for success as nurses of the future by helping to transmit evidence-based knowledge, develop comprehensive assessment skills and encourage positive, empowering attitudes so that they can provide the care that health and social care providers, patients, residents, clients and their families expect. BiographySara’s background embraces both the Arts and Science. As a Classics graduate from the University of London, Sara worked in educational publishing before undertaking a Bachelor of Nursing at the University of Technology, Sydney and beginning her nursing career. During this time, she identified her interest in palliative care, from which specialisation she could explore the perenial questions surrounding living and dying, health and ill health, and what matters as we face ageing and dying. An output of Sara's Bachelor of Nursing studies was a chapter 'Spirituality in Palliative Care' written within a resource for nurse practitioners entering the speciality of palliative care.

Sara’s clinical background is palliative care nursing across specialist, acute and community palliative care services. Sara’s PhD (2018) research focused on the residential aged care workforce and the development of an instrument to evaluate the knowledge, skills and attitudes of nursing assistants (unlicensed health care workers) providing a palliative approach to older people in residential aged care facilities. Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr. Sheree Armistead is an Australian Research Council DECRA fellow at CODES (Centre for Ore Deposit and Earth Sciences), where she investigates the interplay between plate tectonics and mineral systems, focusing on their cyclical and long-term changes throughout Earth’s history. Her expertise spans isotope geochemistry, data science, GIS, and plate reconstruction techniques to unravel the processes that shape mineral systems over geological timescales.

Sheree's DECRA fellowship is titled The interplay of tectonics and climate on critical minerals in deep time. This project seeks to address the urgent need for critical minerals by identifying tectonic and climatic conditions favorable for forming sediment-hosted copper and cobalt deposits over the last billion years. Using samples from the Central African Copperbelt—the world’s largest sediment-hosted Cu-Co district—alongside cutting-edge plate tectonic models, global sedimentary basin datasets, and geochemical tools, this research aims to provide innovative predictive frameworks for locating ore deposits in Australia and globally.

Sheree joined UTAS as a Postdoctoral Researcher and Lecturer in 2022, where she has led and contributed to several research projects, including a collaborative project with Geoscience Australia on the tectonic and metallogenic evolution of western Tasmania. Her work bridges the gap between fundamental geoscience research and its practical applications in mineral exploration.

Before joining UTAS, Sheree undertook a two-year Postdoctoral Research Fellowship at the Geological Survey of Canada in Ottawa, funded through the Metal Earth program at Laurentian University. This project used a global database of Pb isotopes from ore deposits to understand early Earth geodynamics and plate tectonics, with implications for ore-forming regions, particularly the Superior Province in Canada.

Sheree completed her PhD at the University of Adelaide in 2019, focusing on the tectonic evolution of supercontinent Gondwana, with a specific emphasis on Madagascar. Her research used isotope geochemistry, structural geology, and geodata analytics to constrain the paleogeography of Madagascar and neighboring regions throughout several supercontinent cycles. This work contributed to refining global plate reconstructions spanning the past billion years.

Prior to her PhD, Sheree worked at Geoscience Australia as a Geochronologist and Mineral Systems Geologist after earning a BSc (Honours) from Monash University.

Supervisor: Doctor Tamieka Pearce

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr. Tamieka Pearce is a Research Fellow at the Tasmanian Institute of Agriculture (TIA), specialising in genetics and molecular plant pathology. Her work underpins the productivity and sustainability of Tasmania’s horticultural industries. Since completing her PhD in 2016, she has focused on plant disease research in crops including pyrethrum, poppies, cherries, and blueberries. Her research has attracted more than $3.6 million in funding, with a third of this secured through projects she has led as Chief Investigator.
Tamieka currently leads a pyrethrum flowering physiology research program aimed at reducing the crop growing season from 18 months to 10 months. This program integrates the identification of early-flowering plants, assessment of heritability, development of tissue culture techniques, and the use of genomic and transcriptome analyses to identify candidate genes in the juvenile–adult transition pathway. In 2023, she was awarded an ARC Early Career Industry Fellowship to advance this research, becoming the only UTAS recipient in the inaugural fellowship round.
In addition to her ARC Fellowship, Tamieka leads an Agricultural Development Fund project (NRE TAS) developing a rapid molecular method for detecting fungal pathogens in pyrethrum leaves. She also supervises three PhD students.
She was selected for the 2023 CoSE Future Research Leaders Program and the 2025 Sciences and Engineering Elevate Program. In 2024, she received both the CoSE Early Career Researcher Award and the Vice-Chancellor’s Early Career Researcher Award. She is also an active member of TIA’s Inclusion, Diversity, and Equity Committee.
Beyond her professional achievements, Tamieka is committed to promoting diversity in agricultural science and to inspiring the next generation of researchers. She balances her career with running a cattle stud with her partner, Lachy, and their two young boys, Austin and Harvie, at their family farm

Bio: Dr. Til Baalisampang is a senior lecturer and researcher specialising in Maritime Systems and Safety Engineering at the Australian Maritime College (AMC), University of Tasmania. He actively works for the Maritime Infrastructure Integrity and Environment (MarIInE) Laboratory, which enables the assessment of the structural integrity of maritime assets and their relationship and impacts on the marine environment. With over five years of academic experience, Dr. Baalisampang has made impactful contributions to the field through his teaching and extensive research.Dr. Baalisampang holds a PhD in Maritime Engineering from the University of Tasmania (2019). He also completed a Bachelor of Engineering (Marine & Offshore Engineering) with Honors from the same institution in 2014. Before migrating to Australia, he completed a Bachelor of Science (2006) from the University of North Bengal, India, recognised as equivalent to an Australian Bachelor of Science by the Australian Overseas Qualification Authority. Since July 2019, Dr. Baalisampang has been a lecturer at the AMC, where he is responsible for delivering Thermal Engineering, Design of Offshore Systems, Special Topics in Ocean Engineering, and Management of Engineering Projects. He is also supervising several PhD students, focusing on the safety and sustainability of offshore systems, including renewable energy systems and hydrogen. His earlier roles include a sessional lecturer and tutor, as well as a final year research mentor at the AMC, where he provided critical guidance and support to undergraduate and postgraduate students.Dr. Baalisampang has an impressive portfolio of research, with numerous publications in high-impact journals. His work primarily focuses on the safety and risk assessment of offshore and marine engineering systems. Notable publications include studies on fire impact assessment in FLNG processing facilities, LNG spill dispersion, drag reduction, hydrogen safety, and safety evaluations in maritime transportation. In addition to his academic roles, Dr. Baalisampang has international research experience, including a six-month internship at the Centre for Risk Integrity and Safety Engineering (c-RISE) at Memorial University of Newfoundland, Canada. During this period, he conducted research on LNG spill dispersion and its impact modellings, which were published in peer-reviewed journals. Prior to moving to Tasmania, from 2006- 2009 he served as a Mathematics and Science teacher at Saraswati Secondary English Boarding School in Dhanusha, Nepal. In this role, he taught Mathematics and Science to grades 8, 9, and 10, managed and conducted student examinations, and worked as a facility manager in the science laboratory.Dr. Baalisampang's contributions have been recognised through several awards and grants, including the Rob Lewis Award for Excellence in Postgraduate Research (2020), the Young Gastech Award (2017) and a Teaching Merit Certificate (2023). He is a member of prestigious organizations such as the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, Engineers Australia, and the Golden Key International Honour Society. Dr. Baalisampang actively contributes to the academic community as a reviewer for several high-impact journals in his field. Dr. Til Baalisampang is a dedicated academic and researcher with a strong background in maritime systems and safety engineering. His experience, coupled with his passion for teaching and research, positions him as a significant contributor to the field and a valuable asset to the Australian Maritime College and the broader engineering community.

Supervisor: Doctor Waqas Hassan

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Waqas Hassan is a Senior Lecturer in the School of Engineering and the Program Leader for Power Electronics and Control at the Centre for Renewable Energy and Power Systems (CREPS), University of Tasmania. He is the Graduate Research Coordinator (GRC) in the School of Engineering and the specialisation coordinator for the undergraduate (UG) Electrical Power and postgraduate (PG) Renewable Energy programs at UTAS. He is a Senior Member of IEEE and currently serves as the Chair of the IEEE Tasmania Subsection and the Counsellor of the IEEE Student Branch Tasmania, Australia. He also serves as an Associate Editor for the IEEE Transactions on Industry Applications.

With a career spanning over 10 years in academia, research, and industry, he brings a distinctive blend of theoretical knowledge and practical engineering expertise to his role. Dr Hassan excels at analysing complex engineering problems and delivering practical, impactful solutions, particularly in the fields of electrical power and renewable energy systems.
Dr Hassan's research interests focus on the design and development of renewable energy technologies and products, renewable power systems, power electronics, battery storage and grid integration, power system control and stability, solar photovoltaic systems, microgrids, hydrogen energy, motor drives, and electric vehicle systems. He leverages his expertise to develop innovative, sustainable energy solutions, addressing the world's growing energy demands through climate-safe engineering practices to enable a more resource-efficient and sustainable future. His work aims to transform our current electricity infrastructure into a smart, sustainable, and resilient system with zero emissions.Prior to joining the University of Tasmania, Dr Hassan worked as a senior engineer at Regal Rexnord Corporation, where he led power electronics research and design projects and successfully developed and commercialised new industrial products, including a next-generation power inverter, demonstrating his capability to bridge innovative research with practical industry implementation. Additionally, he has also served as a casual lecturer at Monash University, Australia.
Following his PhD completion, Dr Hassan held a postdoctoral research position at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), Australia. During his doctoral studies, he actively engaged with the academic community, working as a casual academic lecturer and tutor at the University of Sydney. Driven by his passion for teaching, he spent six years as a full-time university lecturer at Sir Syed CASE Institute of Technology, Pakistan. In this role, he coordinated and taught undergraduate and postgraduate courses, conducted research, and supervised honours and postgraduate students. His enduring passion for teaching and research continues to shape his contributions to the field of renewable energy and power systems.

Bio: Dr Wenli Yang is a Lecturer in the School of Information and Communication Technology at the University of Tasmania. She holds two PhDs—one in System Analysis and Integration from Huazhong University of Science and Technology (2012) and another in Computer Engineering from the University of Tasmania (2022). Her career spans across China, the United States, and Australia, with experience in both academic and industry roles. Before joining UTAS in 2017, she worked as a research scholar at the University of California, Davis, and spent five years as an associate telecommunications engineer focusing on intelligent transport systems. Her transition from industry to academia, supported by dual doctoral qualifications, highlights a unique and productive research trajectory shaped by real-world challenges and technical depth.

Dr Yang has extensive experience in applied AI research and leadership, with a strong record of success in both academic and industry-linked projects. Her research spans image processing, machine learning and deep learning, knowledge representation and reasoning, explainable AI, and generative AI. She focuses on building AI models that are robust, scalable, and adaptable, designed to operate reliably across varied data sources and real-world conditions.

Dr Yang has strong experience working with government, academic, and industry partners. She collaborates with organisations such as the Australian Antarctic Data Centre, CSIRO, Australian Seafood Industries, Tasmanian Fisheries, and Nocturnal Wildlife Research, among others. These partnerships support cross-disciplinary research and have led to the development of AI-driven systems for areas including marine monitoring, aquaculture automation, environmental sensing, and Antarctic data integration.

Dr Yang teaches across undergraduate, Honours, and postgraduate levels, coordinating units in artificial intelligence, data science, and research methods. Her teaching approach blends real-world tools, industry engagement, and experiential learning. She has developed innovative and industry-aligned materials, receiving consistently positive feedback. Her experience includes unit coordination, material development, and the integration of authentic assessments that reflect professional practice for applied technologies.

Dr Yang serves as the Honours Coordinator. In this role, she supports honour and master research pathway students in navigating their academic journeys and fosters a positive and inclusive environment for their professional development. She actively mentors students at all stages of their research journey, helping them explore supervisors, identify suitable topics, navigate proposal development, and connect with interdisciplinary opportunities.

text:
Supervisor: Doctor William Connelly

Role: Doctor

School: Tasmanian School of Medicine

Sub-organisation: Medicine

Bio: Highlights
After more than a decade studying the computations performed by biological neural circuits, Dr William Connelly's research has shifted from understanding intelligence in the brain to building intelligent systems. His work now focuses on applied artificial intelligence and machine learning, developing models that solve practical problems in medicine, neuroscience and conservation. His research spans computer vision, deep learning, time-series analysis and explainable AI, with applications including human movement analysis, medical decision support, and embedded AI systems for wildlife conservation. Recent projects include the development of edge AI systems capable of identifying Tasmanian devils in the field to support automated vaccine delivery for the conservation of this endangered species.
Dr Connelly's interest in machine learning grew directly out of his background as a neuroscientist. Having spent years studying biological neural networks, he was fascinated by the idea of constructing artificial ones: systems whose internal computations could be examined and understood in complete detail. Training his first neural network to recognise handwritten digits was a turning point. Watching a collection of simple mathematical operations learn to solve a problem without being explicitly programmed convinced him that machine learning would become one of the defining technologies of modern science. Since then, he has applied AI across a diverse range of biomedical and ecological problems, combining a strong quantitative background with practical experience developing, training and deploying deep learning models. His current research emphasises building reliable AI systems that can operate outside the laboratory, from wearable health technologies to low-power embedded devices deployed in remote environments.
BiographyDr William Connelly completed his PhD at the University of Otago, NZ, where he used electrophysiology to study inhibitory neurotransmission in the central nervous system. He then took up a post-doctoral position with Prof. Vincenzo Crunelli, Cardiff University, UK, where he worked on the physiology of thalamocortical neurons. He then took up a position working with Prof Greg Stuart, Australian National University, where he worked on trying to understand synaptic integration in the visual cortex.In 2018 he took up a Lectureship at the University of Tasmania.

Research fields: Sensory systems, Machine learning, Neurosciences, Biomedical and clinical sciences, Information and computing sciences

Bio: Dr William Reay is a senior research fellow in Statistical Genetics and leads the Neurodegeneration and Psychiatric Genomics Research Group at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research. Bio: Brad Sutherland is a Professor in the Medical Sciences Program of the Tasmanian School of Medicine. His main research interests focus on the regulation of the microvascular system, how it is controlled at the cellular and molecular level, and how this becomes dysfunctional in diseases such as stroke, dementia and multiple sclerosis. He also teaches Neuroscience and Physiology into a number of units as part of the BBiomed and BSc degrees.BiographyBrad completed his PhD at the University of Otago (Dunedin, New Zealand) where he investigated the activation of inflammatory pathways in the brain after stroke. After a small stint as a Teaching Fellow in Pharmacology & Toxicology (University of Otago), he took up a Post-doctoral Research Fellowship with the Acute Stroke Programme, Radcliffe Department of Medicine, University of Oxford (Oxford, UK). During his time in Oxford, he formed an interest in the regulation of blood flow in the brain in health and disease. This led to studies investigating the interaction between brain tissue and the blood vessels, the signalling mechanisms that controlled energy delivery to the brain, and how these were disrupted in conditions such as stroke.In mid-2016, Brad arrived at the University of Tasmania to build the Perivascular Research Group and continue investigating the control of cerebral blood flow and blood-brain barrier function with a focus on pericytes. He also has projects looking into dysfunction of the neurovascular unit in brain diseases such as stroke, Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, multiple sclerosis and chronic fatigue syndrome. and build the Perivascular Research Group. He continues to use a wide range of in vitro and in vivo models to assess mechanisms of neurovascular regulation and models of disease.

text:
Supervisor: Professor Eloise Foo

Role: Professor

School: School of Natural Sciences

Sub-organisation: Biological Sciences

Bio: Some plants have advantages over others – they have relationships with bacteria and fungi that allow them to get additional nutrients from the air and soil. Researcher Dr Eloise Foo is studying pea plants to find out why they have these special relationships. If we were free from needing to use fertilisers, and instead could use bacteria and fungi to provide plant nutrients to large-scale crops such as wheat, rice and corn, it could be a game-changer for global agriculture.The holy grail of plant fertilisersDiscovery research, or pure science, involves working out how things work, which helps us to find new tools that can be applied to solve other problems.'I'm studying how plants gain access to the things they need—the nutrients and building blocks of life. They get energy from the sun but they need nutrients, which they mainly take up through their roots, either directly or by associating with bacteria and fungi that help them get nutrients out of the soil,' said Dr Foo. 'Only some plants can form these special symbiotic relationships with bacteria and fungi. Pea is one of these plants. We're lucky at the University of Tasmania to have expertise in studying peas and their growth hormones.'Plants need nitrogen, which is abundant in the atmosphere; however, they can't absorb it that way. This is why most gardeners and commercial growers add nitrogen fertiliser to their soils. I'm working on understanding how bacteria work with some plants to draw nitrogen out of the air and make it available to the plant. Importantly this very specialised plant–bacteria relationship shares similarities with another much more widespread plant–fungi association to access phosphate, another important nutrient for plant growth. By understanding both the differences and similarities, we hope to expand plant-bacterial associations into major crops.'Plants possess growth hormones in minute quantities. Measuring them is our speciality here at the University of Tasmania, and our researchers have developed this expertise over many decades. We have a vast store of special pea mutants on campus, and with our expertise in developmental genetics we can compete nationally and internationally to get funding and to be published.'… there wouldn't be any need for nitrogen fertilisers. This is the holy grail.'Dr Foo believes that if they can uncover the special relationship peas have with their bacteria and fungi they might unlock information that could be used for other plants.Dr Eloise Foo is an ARC Future Fellow at the School of Biological Sciences. She is interested in how plants interact with their environment and how this is regulated by plant hormones: small, mobile, potent signals. In addition to Future Fellowship, she holds an ARC grant at aims to decode the signals important for plant-microbe interactions. She has contributed to the discovery of and current understanding of the newest plant hormone group, strigolactones, and has defined novel roles for plant hormones in plants relationships with beneficial and pathogenic microbes.BiographyEloise completed her undergraduate and PhD at the University of Queensland, working with Professor Christine Beveridge's group investigating the hormones controlling shoot architecture. She then joined the University of Tasmania, working with Professor Jim Reid and Dr Jim Weller examining plant responses to light. She secured an ARC Early career Fellowship that enabled her to create a research focus at UTAS examining the role of plant hormones in interactions with beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil. She has since expanded this work with her current Future Fellowship to encompass plant hormones role in plant-microbe interactions, including nitrogen-fixing bacteria and soil pathogens.Career summaryQualifications PhD - University of Queensland (2004) Title of thesis: The genetic control of branching in peaMembershipsCommittee associations Australasian Plant Pathology Society Inc. Australian Society of Plant ScientistsAdministrative expertiseEloise has experience managing a large ARC Discovery grant, including supervision of post-doctoral fellows, research staff and post-graduate students.

Bio: Jan McDonald is the New Star Professor of Environmental and Climate Law. She holds degrees in Arts and Law, with first class Honours in Law, from the University of Queensland. text:
Supervisor: Professor Kathryn Burdon

Role: Professor

School: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Sub-organisation: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Bio: HighlightsIn Australia, around one in every fifty people suffers from blindness or vision impairment that cannot be corrected by glasses. This proportion is expected to grow as the Australian population ages. Among Australians aged 55 years and older, around 10 per cent experience vision loss and blindness.Professor Kathryn Burdon at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research studies the genetic factors involved in eye diseases that cause loss of vision. Genes are known to play a role in some of the most common eye diseases – like glaucoma, cataracts and diabetic retinopathy. This genetic link is particularly strong in diseases that affect children and young adults, like childhood cataracts and keratoconus, a disease of the cornea at the front of the eye. In diseases that affect older people, the causes tend to be a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors.‘Having a detailed understanding of the genetic risk factors involved in each disease of the eye can make a tremendous difference,’ Professor Burdon says. ‘Where specific genetic mutations are known to be linked with eye diseases, we can screen people who are at risk. Identifying people with the mutation before they start showing symptoms allows us to intervene with treatments at an early stage.’For diseases where the genetic causes are not known, Professor Burdon and her team carry out ‘gene discovery’. ‘We do whole genome sequencing where we investigate the entire genetic material – the DNA – of people with and without the diseases. We then compare this huge amount of information using the Menzies Institute’s supercomputer to see what is different in the genes of people with the disease.’For their research, Professor Burdon and her colleagues at the Menzies Institute maintain the Tasmanian Ophthalmic Biobank. It contains blood or saliva samples donated by people with and without eye diseases from which DNA can be extracted. ‘This is a fantastic resource for the kind of research my team does.’Tasmania is a particularly good place to do research into the genetic factors involved in disease. ‘Tasmania has a relatively stable population with many large extended families and with good population records over many generations, going all the way back to the convict records. By combining our genetic analysis with these population records, we can trace the inheritance of particular genetic variations through several generations of a family and see how they correlate with diseases.’Professor Burdon and her team take their research a step further. ‘We not only try to work out what genetic variations are associated with what diseases. We also investigate the role of that gene in healthy people and the precise mechanism by which the variation causes the disease.’ This detailed understanding opens up the possibility of developing new drug-based treatments.Another area of research is looking at how the success of existing therapies is affected by genetic and environmental factors. For example, anti-VEGF – a common treatment for macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy – is only successful in about 50 per cent of patients. ‘We are studying patients going through the 12-month course of treatment with anti-VEGF to see how particular genes, but also the frequency of injections and the severity of the disease before treatment starts, affect success rates. Knowing this will allow us to better target treatment to patients who will benefit from it.’The thrill of discovery motivates Professor Burdon’s research. ‘It’s a thrill to know you have found something truly new. For a short while you are the only person in the world to know something important and then you share your discovery with the world.’‘It’s especially exciting when you know your research can directly improve the quality of life of so many people.’CareerProfessor Burdon is a molecular geneticist with an interest in ophthalmic genetics. Her research focuses on the identification and characterization of genes and variants that lead to blinding eye diseases. She also works on multiple sclerosis and cardiovascular genetics in collaboration with others at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research.BiographyProfessor Burdon received a PhD in 2004 from the University of Tasmania in genetics of paediatric cataract and completed postdoctoral training at the Human Genome Centre of Wake Forest University, North Carolina, USA. As an NHMRC Peter Doherty Fellow, Dr Burdon established a laboratory at Flinders University focused on the identification and characterisation of genes causing inherited eye disease including glaucoma and cataract. In 2014 Dr Burdon returned to the University of Tasmania as an NHMRC Senior Research Fellow and is now Professorial Research Fellow and Deputy Director at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research. Current research focuses on the identification of genes for inherited eye disease and the use of that knowledge in clinical care. Professor Burdon is a highly experienced researcher with broad ranging skills relating to human genetics, including sequencing, bioinformatics, molecular biology, disease model systems and variant interpretation. Prof Burdon’s research has led to the identification of novel genes, causative variants and genetic risk factors for many eye diseases including cataract, glaucoma, keratoconus and diabetic retinopathy.Career summaryQualificationsPhD, Investigations of Cataract Genetics, University of Tasmania, Australia 24/12/2003BSc(Hons) Albinism genes and congenital esotropia, University of Tasmania, Australia 1999MembershipsCommittee associationsChair of Scientific Program Committee, Human Genetics Society of AustralasiaClinGen Glaucoma Variant Curation Expert Panel MemberOtherSection Editor 'Genetics', Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology (2014-current)Human Genetics Society of AustralasiaAustralian Genomics Technologies AssociationAmerican Society for Human GeneticsInternational Society for Eye ResearchAssociation for Research in Vision and OphthalmologyAdministrative expertiseMenzies Institute for Medical Research Theme Leader: Genetics and CancerMenzies Institute for Medical Research Lead Graduate Research Co-ordinator

Bio: Mark Hovenden is a plant ecologist with a particular interest in linking how plant communities are comprised, how the plants within the community interact and how the behaviour of individual plants all lead to the function of the entire ecosystem. Both his teaching and research activities are directed towards understanding the way that plant communities and terrestrial ecosystems actually work and how and the non-living environment, particularly climate, controls ecosystem functioning. Unless we understand how ecosystems actually function, we cannot hope to manage them in a rapidly changing world, so a primary motivation for Mark's career has been to improve the way we manage the planet, starting locally and aiming globally. An extremely important component of his career is the use of manipulative field experiments supported by a broad range of approaches, from studying the responses of individual plants right up to studying how the whole ecosystem responds. Linking these measurements in the field, with a range of manipulations in relatively long-term experiments, provides a comprehensive and mechanistic assessment of ecosystem function.BiographyMark began his interest in botany as a child on caravanning holidays with his family in the bush across eastern Australia. He studied botany at the University of Sydney, studying fire ecology and later spending two years as a research assistant working on mangroves. He then moved to Tasmania in 1991 to work at the Australian Antarctic Division as a research scientist investigating terrestrial ecology of lichens of the Windmill Islands, near Casey Station, for which work he received his PhD from the University of Tasmania in 1996. Prof Hovenden then spent a year working on low temperature effects on eucalypts at the Terrestrial Hardwood Forestry CRC in Hobart before returning to the School of Plant Science as an ARC Postdoctoral Fellow working on the impacts of climate on leaf form and growth of the southern beech, Nothofagus cunninghamii. Bio: I am a Laureate Fellow of the Australian Research Council and Professor of Polar Geodesy at the University of Tasmania, Australia. I also have the pleasure of being Director of the Australian Centre for Excellence in Antarctic Science (www.antarctic.org.au).

My Laureate Fellowship focuses on tracking and predicting the future of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. Starting from 2026, I will be building a team of about 12 postdocs and PhD students and working with a great team of collaborators in Australia and overseas. We will work on improving estimates of surface mass balance, observations of mass and elevation change, modelling and observing glacial isostatic adjustment, and ice sheet modelling.
My background:
After completing my PhD at the University of Tasmania in geodesy/glaciology I worked within one of Europe’s leading geodesy groups at the University of Newcastle upon Tyne from 2002-2012. During that time, I progressed from Junior Research Associate to Full Professor while working on problems within academia and industry. In late 2012, I returned to the University of Tasmania as Professor of Polar Geodesy. Through my career I have been supported by competitive research fellowships (NERC Postdoctoral Fellowship, RCUK Academic Fellowship, ARC Future Fellowship, and now ARC Laureate Fellowship).During my career, I have been able to work with outstanding colleagues from across geodesy, glaciology, solid Earth sciences, oceanography and many other fields. I have received a number of prestigious prizes and fellowships, including from the Royal Society of London and the Australian Academy of Sciences.Collaboration:I’ve been blessed to work with some wonderful early (and senior!) career researchers from many countries, including a great group of PhD students and postdocs. We work in a collaborative way to try and tackle problems that are of importance to populations globally. text:
Supervisor: Professor Michael Breadmore

Role: Professor

School: School of Natural Sciences

Sub-organisation: Chemistry

Bio: Analytical chemistry rewards creative thinkers who see opportunities, not barriers, between disciplines, according to Professor Michael Breadmore. Michael and his team at the University of Tasmania are developing 'lab-on-a-chip' portable analytical devices that allow users to put a sample in and get an answer out on the spot. These devices have the potential to revolutionise clinical, forensic, environmental and industrial applications. Lab-on-a-chip technology Analytical chemistry goes out of the lab for real-world, real-time analysis Professor Michael Breadmore is an analytical chemist and former ARC Fellow (QPD, QEII, FT) at the University of Tasmania's College of Sciences and Engineering. Quick to dispel any ideas that analytical chemists have a limited research field, Professor Breadmore points out, 'I use ideas and technology from all kinds of areas. You can see this best in what's been nicknamed 'lab-on-a-chip' technology, which involves measuring complex mixtures of chemicals on a miniature scale. 'My recent interests have focused on out-of-lab systems to provide timely chemical information for a range of applications. Rapid, screening of explosives, illicit drugs and pharmacueticals, is important where the information needs to be obtained within minutes to make an informed a decision. Likewise, autonomus and continuous collection of data over longer periods of time is important to construct spatio-temporal maps of our water chemistry and how it is changing over time. The timeframe upon which the information is needed always defines our technical solution.' 'You need to be creative to do this work [Some of our] best breakthroughs have come from pursuing ideas that might be considered crazy. I encourage that.''The more creative you are, the more interesting and exciting research you can do. You still need to be able to think in a logical and structural manner, but my own and my team's best breakthroughs have come from pursuing ideas that might be considered crazy. I encourage that.'Professor Breadmore and his team have developed two systems that have made it to market. Grey Scan's ETD-100 is the first and only instrumentat in the world to detect the full range of homemade inorganic explosives. Eco Detections Ion-Q provides continuous monitoring of upto 14 water chemistry parameters.'My advice to new researchers is to keep working on the things that shouldn't work - ignore the boundaries other people impose on your area of research. Forget working outside the box - there is no box.' Fast-fact: Professor Breadmore, along with colleague Professor Emily Hilder, were two of only three Australian academics to be recognised in Analytical Scientist magazine's inaugural Top 40 Under 40 Power List in 2014. Since then, he has featured frequently in their power list as a global influencer in analytical chemistry.Professor Breadmore received his PhD in 2001 from the University of Tasmania before undertaking his first postdoctoral position at the University of Virginia, USA to work on portable analytical technology for genetic diagnostics. He then moved to the Institute of Clinical Pharmacology at the University of Bern, Switzerland, where he developed electrophoretic methods for therapeutic drug monitoring of anti-fungal and retroviral drugs, with the methods implemented routinely in the adjacent hospital service lab. He then spent eight months working with delta DOT, a small biotechnology instrumentation company, and helped design their commercial capillary electrophoresis instrument. In 2004, Professor Breadmore returned to Australia as an ARC postdoctoral fellow, in 2009 was awarded an ARC QEII Fellowship and in 2014 began an ARC Future Fellowship.

Research fields: Theoretical and computational chemistry not elsewhere classified, Instrumental methods (excl. immunological and bioassay methods), Separation science, Theoretical and computational chemistry, Chemical sciences, Analytical chemistry

text:
Supervisor: Professor Seana Gall

Role: Professor

School: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Sub-organisation: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Bio: Highlights

Prof Seana Gall is an epidemiologist that studies the risk factors and outcomes for heart disease and strokes.As a cardiovascular epidemiologist, she works with large sets of data and looks for answers to important questions like: what is the frequency of a particular disease and how is that frequency changing over time? Are there groups within the population that suffer higher rates of the disease? What are the factors that make these diseases more or less likely? And what are the factors that affect the outcomes of treatment? One area of Prof Gall’s research is to examine the factors that put certain groups within the population at a higher risk of heart disease and stroke. Overall, statistics have shown a gradual decline in the incidence of stroke and heart disease. However, among some groups such as young people and women, this trend has levelled off in recent years and even shifted into reverse.‘Understanding the factors driving these trends will allow us to develop better approaches to disease prevention,’ Prof Gall says. ‘This might include better and more targeted education about the risk factors and designing more effective programs or policies for early intervention to prevent strokes and heart disease.’In her research, Prof Gall draws on several large cohort studies. This includes the Childhood Determinants of Adult Health study (CDAH) – an Australia-wide study that follows up on people first assessed when they were at school in 1985. ‘The CDAH study allows us to take a life-course approach and investigate the importance of childhood factors in the later development of risk factors for heart disease and stroke, factors like weight, diet, physical activity and smoking.‘As an epidemiologist, I find Tasmania is a particularly good place to do this kind of work,’ Prof Gall says. ‘Being an island state means it is easier to keep track of people over the course of a long-term study. Also, unfortunately, some of the risk factors we are studying are particularly prevalent in Tasmania.’A large part Prof Gall’s research is investigating how to prevent stroke, which happens when the blood supply to the brain is stopped. 'Stroke is a large cause of death and ill health in Tasmania' Prof Gall says. 'It can happen to people of any age but it is preventable, with up to 8 out of 10 strokes thought to be preventable by managing the risk factors for stroke like high blood pressure or smoking' . She recently led Australia’s first research program dedicated to stroke prevention – Synergies to Prevent Stroke (STOPstroke) – funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council’s Synergy Grant program for $5 million over 5 years (2020-2025). Prof Gall and her team of collaborators across Australia and New Zealand are searching for new ways to prevent strokes. 'We are running several studies to develop and test new ways to help people know and manage their risk factors for stroke. We are also working with people that have had a stroke to find better tools and programs so that people can lower their risk factors and stop them having another stroke' says Prof Gall. Prof Gall’s wide expertise has seen her appointed to several public health bodies. She chairs the Tobacco Control Coalition – a Tasmanian government initiative that also involves NGOs – that is responsible for developing the state’s tobacco control plan, including setting goals and priorities, developing plans and overseeing the implementation of those plans. She is a member of the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's Cardiovascular Disease Expert Group and current Treasurer for the Australian and New Zealand Stroke Organisation.

Research fields: Cardiology (incl. cardiovascular diseases), Epidemiology not elsewhere classified, Health informatics and information systems, Cardiovascular medicine and haematology, Biomedical and clinical sciences, Epidemiology, Health sciences, Health services and systems

Role: Professor

School: School of Humanities and Social Sciences

Sub-organisation: The Forest Building

Bio: Vaughan Higgins is a Professor of Sociology and Head of the Sociology and Criminology Program in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. Since graduating from his PhD in 2001, Vaughan’s research has focused on the forms of governance – including policies, programs, standards, technologies – and organisational arrangements that contribute to more sustainable and secure agri-food industries in Australia. Informed by analytical approaches such as assemblage thinking, actor network theory, and governmentality, Vaughan’s work has been important in highlighting the often nuanced and subtle ways in which agri-food governance is navigated and made to work in local and regional contexts.

For the past 15 years, much of Vaughan’s research has focused on Australia’s biosecurity system, with a particular interest in the implementation of a shared responsibility approach. His work in this area has examined the institutional logics shaping how diverse biosecurity stakeholders engage with shared responsibility, as well as the practices through which biosecurity compliance is made workable in farming regions. Vaughan’s research on biosecurity has informed national agricultural policy and strategy. His expertise has played a key role in shaping Australia’s biosecurity future through membership of the Federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry’s National Biosecurity Strategy Working Group and, more recently, the National Biosecurity Strategy Implementation Committee.

Vaughan joined the University of Tasmania in January 2018 as an Associate Professor. He commenced his academic career in 2000 as an Associate Lecturer (part-time) at Monash University. In 2011 he was appointed as an Associate Professor in the School of Humanities and Social Science at Charles Sturt University. During his career, Vaughan has had several international engagements, including visiting appointments at Cardiff University and Imperial College London.

Research fields: Rural sociology, Sociology, Human society

Role: Professor

School: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Sub-organisation: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Bio: Professor Verity Cleland is a public health researcher, educator, and advisor with deep expertise in population health, health promotion, and applied research translation. Based at the University of Tasmania, she brings more than a decade of experience leading complex research projects, supervising postgraduate students, and working collaboratively with government, community organisations, and health services.

Professor Cleland's research focuses on understanding how where we live, work, study, and play can impact physical activity, and on developing population level strategies to increase activity. Her work focuses on generating and applying evidence to improve health outcomes, particularly through rigorous research design, program evaluation, and the translation of findings into policy and practice. She works closely with partners from diverse disciplines to ensure her research is highly relevant to policy and practice. Verity is known for her ability to distil complex information into clear, actionable insights — a skill she applies in grant development, research capacity‑building, and advisory roles. She is an invited member of international, national, and local funding panels, peer reviews for many academic journals, and regularly examines PhD theses.

She is widely recognised for her supportive, collaborative approach and her commitment to building research capability across the health and community sectors. She is Chair of the Tasmanian Premier’s Health and Wellbeing Advisory Council, where she advises the Premier on best practices approaches to improving health and wellbeing, and the Tasmanian Active Living Coalition, where she brings together professionals across academia, planning, local government, state government, advocacy, and transport to connect and advocate for environments that support active living. The impact of her work has been recognised through numerous awards, including a Paul Dudley White Scholar Award at the American Heart Association's Epi | Lifestyle scientific meeting (2019) and institutional Research Impact (2024), Academic Mentoring (2023), Engagement (2021), and Best Publication (2022) awards.

Research fields: Health promotion, Public health not elsewhere classified, Behavioural epidemiology, Cardiology (incl. cardiovascular diseases), Public health, Health sciences, Epidemiology, Cardiovascular medicine and haematology, Biomedical and clinical sciences

Bio: Professor Wang has an internationally recognised research profile in thermodynamics, cooling engineering, desalination, energy storage and conversion, battery thermal management, and renewable energy utilization. He is a Fellow of Engineers Australia and a member of the World Society of Sustainable Energy Technologies. He received the DAAD Visiting Scholar from the German Academic Exchange Service in 2003 and the Ludwig Mond Prize from the Institution of Mechanical Engineers (IMechE), United Kingdom, in 2005. He was selected for the Australia–China Young Scientist Exchange Program (2009) and the Australia–Japan Emerging Research Leader Program (2016) by the Australian Academy of Technological Sciences and Engineering. He received the Dean’s Award for Outstanding Research Performance (2016) and the UTAS College Award for Research Excellence (2023) from the University of Tasmania. He has been recognised as a Field Leader in Thermal Sciences by The Australian Research Magazine in 2018 and 2026, and has been listed among the Stanford/Elsevier Top 2% Scientists since 2021. In 2024, he received the Applied Thermal Engineering Editors' Choice Award. He currently serves as Subject Editor for Applied Thermal Engineering and Associate Editor for Scientific Reports and Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part E: Journal of Process Mechanical Engineering. He has also served as a Guest Editor for Applied Sciences and Energies, and is a board member of five other international journals.
BiographyProfessor Wang received his B.Eng and Ph.D. degrees from the Xi'an Jiaotong University, China in 1994 and 1999, respectively. After he worked in the industry in Singapore for three years, he started his academic career as a Research Fellow (A) in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, the National University of Singapore in 2002. In 2003, he was invited by DAAD, Germany to work as a visiting scientist at the University of Siegen, Germany. In 2005, he joined the School of Mechanical and Chemical Engineering, the University of Western Australia as a Lecturer and was promoted to Research Associate Professor in 2009. In July 2012, he joined the School of Engineering, University of Tasmania. Xiaolin has extensive industrial experiences in thermodynamics of cooling and power systems, heat pump technologies, desalination, energy storage and conversion, and renewable energy applications. text:
Supervisor: Professor Zanna Chase

Role: Professor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Sub-organisation: Oceans and Cryosphere

Bio: Zanna Chase is Professor of Chemical Oceanography at the University of Tasmania, Australia. She works within the Oceans and Cryosphere Centre at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. Her research focuses on the interaction between chemical cycles and biological activity in the oceans, and how these are affected by climate. Understanding of these interactions, both in the modern ocean and the paleo-ocean, is necessary to predict the oceans' response and contribution to future climate change.She is particularly interested in the role of the Southern Ocean in long term climate change. In her research, Zanna applies a variety of geochemical proxies in sediment cores, including long-lived, naturally occurring radioisotopes to reconstruct particle flux, and redox-sensitive metals to reconstruct ocean oxygenation. She is also involved in research to improve our understanding of trace metal proxies used in paleoceanography, primarily through participation in the international GEOTRACES program.Zanna is active in research leadership at the University of Tasmania, having served on the IMAS Research Committee for many years, and as the Associate Head of Research for IMAS from 2019 to 2021. Zanna is a sea-going oceanographer, and has participated in over 22 research voyages, many with leadership roles. Her research is complemented by teaching in oceanography and biogeochemistry.BiographyZanna’s contributions to chemical oceanography are primarily in the fields of paleoceanography and biogeochemistry. Her research has often combined these two fields in innovative ways, building on insights from present-day process studies and modelling to understand the past. Zanna studied biology and mathematics as an undergraduate, and then completed a master’s degree in biological oceanography, all at McGill University. She then moved into chemical oceanography and paleoceanography as a PhD student at Columbia University’s Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory. Before joining UTAS and IMAS in 2010, she was on the faculty at Oregon State University.

Research fields: Chemical oceanography, Palaeoclimatology, Climate change science, Oceanography, Earth sciences, Physical geography and environmental geoscience
